items.body:
Tomohiro Kamiyama of WEST. has released his first solo album, INPUT⇄OUTPUT.

The record arrives following the launch of Kamiyama's original solo project in July. Written and produced by Kamiyama himself, INPUT⇄OUTPUT sees the Japanese artist bringing together a genre-spanning collection of tracks shaped by his musical influences and creative output.

Alongside the album release, Kamiyama has unveiled a lyric video for 'No Filter', a rapid-fire rap track featured on the record.

INPUT⇄OUTPUT also includes the previously released 'G.O.D.', which arrived as a surprise on Kamiyama's birthday, as well as collaborations with Sota Hanamura of Da-iCE, KNOCK OUT MONKEY, Daisuke Ozasa of Official Hige Dandism, and Shota Yasuda of SUPER EIGHT.

items.body:
YAO are back with new music.

The collaborative project comprising Awich, CHICO CARLITO, ONE OK ROCK, and Paledusk released their second single, 'FOR OKINAWA', on 4 September.

Born from conversations between the members during the production process, 'FOR OKINAWA' explores Okinawa's history and culture, as well as the lasting scars of its past. Okinawa natives Awich and CHICO CARLITO shared stories about their homeland and the realities faced by those who continue to carry its history.

Their perspectives resonated with the rest of YAO, including ONE OK ROCK's Taka. The Tokyo-born musician came to share their desire for peace and determination to preserve Okinawa's cultural heritage, giving the collective a common purpose behind the track.

For 'FOR OKINAWA', Taka also challenged himself to create a melody unlike anything he had attempted before. The song brings together the members' distinct backgrounds, experiences, and roots around their shared message.

YAO takes its name and inspiration from the Japanese concept of Yaoyorozu, the belief that countless spirits exist in all things. Through the project, the four acts bring together perspectives from hip-hop, rock, mainstream, and underground music in pursuit of new forms of artistic expression.

items.body: We are extremely excited about the Experimental segment of our Fall Music Preview, as it contains all manner of treasures! This fall’s releases include an album that concentrates on the metallic aspects of percussion and other works inspired by biomes, nest building and Haruki Murakami’s IQ84. The youngest performers are in the single digits, while the oldest is an octogenarian. With such a wide variety here on display, there’s something for everyone to enjoy. So set aside all expectations, put those earbuds in and prepare to be dazzled! Our cover image is a lovely collage designed by Sonnenzimmer for Katherine Young‘s BIOMES, covered below. Electroacoustic Lea Bertucci and Michael Beharie may be vying for attention with Sarah Davachi come year’s end, as Bow and Arrow walks through similar glens. Their sound, billed as “electroacoustic spectral folk,” puts one in mind of autumn and its mysterious natural timbres (NNA Tapes, October 23). Weston Olenki and TAK ensemble‘s when the great fires were lit on the other side of the ocean is one of the season’s most distinct recordings, inspired by the writings of W.G. Sebald on electricity and including field recordings from Tesla’s first power plant. The limited edition includes both the score and a lecture packet (Sweet Wreath, September 30). Hallow Ground offers John McCowen‘s Pressure Chords feat. Lucy Railton, Weston Olencki, an album that could just as easily landed in our Drone department. With contrabass clarinet, cello and trombone, the trio stretches tones taffy-thin before rebuilding them layer by layer (September 18). After this comes Jordan Sand‘s Baby Ghost, whose tendrils of falsetto voice are mingled with passages of bowed double bass, producing an otherworldly effect (October 2).   Free improvisation meets metal and drone on Mats Erlandsson & Gus Loxbo‘s Minnets Långa Kedjor (XKatedral, September 18), a moody album with narration from Maria W Horn. At times, the work invokes Swans, which makes sense as Michael Gira offers guest narration on Horn’s own album, Melting Pillars of Snow, out October 2 on the same label. Buy them both to experience the depths of a dark autumn.   Misanthropic Agenda‘s first releases of the season are out today. Vincent Grimaldi‘s Amorcie De Champ is crinkly and dark, a collage of field recordings, turntables and tapes, while the troublingly named Perverts in White Shirts offers “cringe pop” on the 28-track CULTrully appropriate songs and revisited memories (September 4). The creaks, rustles and cracks of Liths (Sarah Hennies, Willie B. and Keir Neuringer) make Ascending the Depths a perfect album for fall, when the shadows creep across the forest floor and strange creatures come out to play (Dinzu Artefacts, September 25).   Mark Peter Wright offers pure North Yorkshire field recordings on Field Crafting, interacting with his environment in a way that honors his surroundings while bringing them to life (Flaming Pines, October 8). Icelandic field recordings decorate the background of Marja Ahti & John McCowen‘s Errands, which fills in the spaces with recorder and clarinet (Black Truffle, September 25). Mixing field recordings with electro-acoustic elements, Crys Cole presents Testing the Waters, a single-track album whose rivers run deep (Persistence of Sound, October 9). Midway between minimalism and drone lies Roel Meelkop‘s Antithesis, a set sounds that relate to each other in interlocking ways (Crónica, September 8). CZN (copper, zinc and nickel) combines the work of percussionist-sculptor João Pais Filipe, composer-drummer Valentina Magaletti, and producer Leon Marks. The concentration on gongs, cymbals and other metal objects earns the trio its moniker, hearkening back to the work of mHz. Parallel Commutator is out October 16 on Oath.   Katherine Young‘s BIOMES is breathy and intense, initially inspired by lichen before expanding into wetlands, oyster reefs and more. Joining the artist: Olivia Block, Ben LaMar Gay, Brian Chase, Tim Daisy, and Yarn/Wire, who help to make the album a three-dimensional experience (Chaikin, September 18). We’re loving the sheets of rain in “Thunder Covered Brush,” the opening track of M. Sage‘s Brush Flier. The artist draws from multiple genres on this album, including ambient, folk and electronic, keeping the dynamic contrast high (RVNG Intl., September 25). ICMC: Best of the Listening Rooms is an electro-acoustic extravaganza, drawing from the 50th anniversary of the International Computer Music Conference. Featuring music from around the world, the compilation is as much a treat for the mind as it is the ears (Ravello, September 18). Yanick Soland is Walking on Rubber Eggshells. The set is a potpourri of sounds: flute, violin, zither, bowed koto and voice. Originally part of a solo exhibition, it displays the “come hither” sound that in person must have drawn people into the room (Futura Resistenza, September 28). Kaoru Watanabe‘s The Arch draws the listener deep into Japanese musical heritage, as the composer plays multiple instruments, including shinobue, ryuteki, hichiriki, taiko, atarigane, suzu, ame uchiwa, and koto, along with some instruments associated with the West. The songs tell stories, teach lessons, and entertain (New Amsterdam, September 18). Using “rage as a creative process,” Marina Herlop presents Dja Dja, which contains multiple nooks and crannies, featuring gamelan, voice and unconventional rhythms, and ultimately comes across as positive. There’s even a t-shirt bundle (October 9).   Jazz and Improvisation 577 Records always has its act together when it comes to pre-orders, which is why they get the lead-off spot. But this season, their first release is a true outlier. Released through the Positive Elevation imprint, the self-titled MY FACE IS DANCING is a family affair ~ specifically, the family of Federico Ughi, who records with his three sons. There’s hip-hop here alongside the jazz, and even some slam poetry: a photo album in sonic form (September 4). Two weeks later, Rafael Zaldivar | McBride | Mela release the languid Meeting in New York, Volume One, which was just recorded this past April (September 18). Savant Fleur follows with the raucous Hocketus, which indulges in dissonance, atonalism and noise, mangling the strings of the cello and violin (September 25). Then the attention turns to the solo work of Cuban musician Francesco Mela, playing multiple instruments on Carnavale De Oriente (October 9). (Mela also has an album out this fall with Nicki Adams and Michael Eaton; Arrival is released on J-Man Records September 10, preceded by the title track.) AIRLFT‘s Spatial Recognition began as a monthly meeting, turned into a community and has now become an album (October 16). We’ll Let You Know When We Find Out, declare Sonelius Smith and Adam Kahan, mixing originals with standards by Monk, Beethoven and Gershwin (October 23). Gon Muruaga leads an international trio on Lines in the Sky, an extremely active recording overflowing with happy notes (October 28). On November 11 we’ll hear FRAGMENTS, from bassist and bandleader Bishu Chattopadhyay, followed a day later by Pat Thomas‘ playful Of all people…, preceded by the highly unusual and engaging “OOPS” (November 12).   Not to be outdone, Endectomorph Music has announced nine fall albums, taking us all the way through December. The fun begins with Christian Li‘s Broken Neon Sign, a mix of instrumental and vocal, improvised and composed (September 4). Then the attention turns to alto saxophonist Kevin Sun for I and II, which includes a cover of “Laura Palmer’s Theme” (September 25). Sunhyun Yoo‘s PLAiDE is filled with sax and decorated with synth and Moog (October 2). Next is the sextet Sundate on October 9, followed by pianist Dabin Ryu and friends on Discomfort. (November 6). Be sure to save room for Matei Predescu‘s Basmeon November 20, Joechen Rueckert’s New Quartet on How to Survive a Beheading (November 20) and Ocelot‘s II on December 4: a generous slate! The Travel Agency Is On Fire is one of the wildest releases of the season. The four-disc box set is a tribute to William S. Burroughs, billed as Anne Waldman, Thurston Moore, James Ilgenfritz, Anagram Ensemble but involving many other guest stars, from Bill Laswell to Tortoise. Fans of spoken word poetry and improv should order on the spot (Infrequent Seams, September 25).   Viola artist Jessica Pavone plays solo on half of …Is In the Air and collaborates on the other half, the best of both worlds (Relative Pitch/Weird Cry, October 16). Given the rather bland title Four Pieces for Viola and Sampler, one might expect the album to be a staid affair; quite the contrary. AJ Nilles & Tom Schneider are often raucous and always wild; you can’t judge an album by the title! (Macro, October 9). Avant cellist Topo Lyo offers quiet scenes from tokyo, embracing bass-like notes with tape loops while constructing humble tributes to nature (Faitiche, November 6). Out of Your Head Records launches autumn with The Realist, showcasing the work of cellist Janel Leppin (September 11). Then it will be time for Mali Obomsawin, the bassist and vocalist leading a nonet on the diverse Automatic (October 16). Next on the docket is acoustic bassist Stephan Crump, who leads a quartet on Passerine, inspired by the work of birds building their nests (October 23). Ambiances Magnétiques has two releases slated for September 25. Érick d’Orion‘s Mes fantômes is thick in some places, thin in others, so that one can hear the phantom threads. Super Scintillant‘s Tarot is jazzier, reflecting the interplay between bass clarinet and modular synthesizer, thanks to Mélanie Bourassa and Nicolas Bernier. Earshift is prepping two releases for September. Awakening is a collection of Armenian music, brought to life by the ensemble Visions of Nar (September 18), while trumpeter Tom Avgenicos leads a quartet on I’ll Go Where You Go as Delay 45, with an emphasis on dynamic contrast (September 25). A large part of Adam Rudolph‘s ensemble is from Türkiye, which results in some fascinating timbres of ney, cuika, waterphone and darbuka. Toys and found objects are also included. Invisible Threads is out on Northern Spy, September 18. Payton MacDonald leads marimba and percussion duos on Transients Vol. 1, 2, & 3, pairing with Susie Ibarra, Billy Martin and Nava Dunkelman (Infrequent Seams, September 4). Baritone saxophonist Tamar Osborn is set to release Varier: Berlin, the first of two albums to be recorded with separate ensembles. (Varier: London will follow next year.) The album is a celebration of the sights and sounds of the city, suffused with an underlying grief and eventual healing as the artist mourns the death of her father (October 2). Duologues 7: Distillation is the latest release from the saxophone and piano duo of Ivo Perelman and Matthew Shipp. Squidco is promising to release a new collaboration every year “in perpetuum” (October 2).   Blair / Huber‘s ECLIPSE is a thoughtful work for saxophone and guitar, the first of an extensive fall slate for LEITER; the rest is under wraps for now (October 16). Liba Villavecchia and Vasco Trilla (sax and drums) make a joyful noise on Serrat, with two side-long jams and album art that reflects the angular sound (defkaz, September 1). Sax and drums duo Nicole McCabe and Savannah Harris offer the warm and friendly All Together Now, prefaced by the single Lonely People, which makes them seem anything but (Sudden Quarterly, September 18). Likely the oldest performer in this article, trumpeter Wadada Leo Smith is still going strong at age 84. Constellations and Hemispheres finds the musician voyaging into inner and outer space with the help of four ensembles, a testament to his versatility (Burning Ambulance, September 25). Also released on Burning Ambulance, trumpeter Michael Sarian presents In This Desert, anchored by the three-part title track, redolent of heat shimmer and wide open spaces (September 25).   Images on loan is the first taste of Yuma Koda‘s enveloping Amid Kinos, which includes appearances from a variety of guest performers on instruments and spoken word. The tone is one of focused calm (Newhere Music, October 2). A similar feeling is created by pianist Kris Davis, leading the Kris Davis Trio on Lost in Geneva, which sounds like being pleasantly found (4166, September 25). Spoken word meets musique concrète on the ambitious Chinese Benefits, recorded on a failing iPhone 6 by A Large Sheet of Muscle (Drowned by Locals, October 16). Pianist Kevin Hays is Live at the Stone. Each of the four pieces includes a guest appearance, which lends the set great tonal variety. One title is “Bob Dylan” (AHT, September 13). Jamie Safir‘s Momentism is playful and warm, a jazzy excursion from a quartet whose sound pairs well with the name of the label (Chill Tone, September 4). A Mind in Motion is the first of Shifting Paradigm‘s fall releases, guitarist Zebu Zheng in charge of a quartet, sounding personal and upbeat (September 18). Following in its wake is Andrew Toombs‘ Alloy; we love the blue and purple cover, along with the laidback grooves (October 16). And we’re not sure how long it takes to make a cake look like a circuit board, but if that’s a photograph on the cover of Twin Talk‘s Delights, color us impressed (October 13). Vibraphonist Jalen Baker leads a nonet on RePaved, a breezy collection of tunes that honors the history of Houston TX’s 3rd, 4th and 5th Wards (Cellar Music, September 4). Bassist Emma Dayhuff leads a septet on Mountains, which seeks to translate the wonder of Montanan vistas into jazz (Division 81, September 4). An eleven-piece ensemble performs A World That Bears a Question, a 28-part suite inspired by Haruki Murakami’s novel 1Q84. One need not read the novel to understand the music of Madre Vaca, but we recommend doing both at once (September 18). Contemporary jazz sextet ONMO offers In Time and Spirit, which draws from myriad influences and “sits outside of jazz time” (Clonmell Jazz Social, October 16). The self-titled album from Oslo ensemble Power Chords is hythmic and percussive, as captured in lead single “Clumsy,” an ironic title as “serendipitous” might make a better description (Sonic Transmissions, October 30). Moon Inhabitants invite you to experience Canned Luna, an exuberant explosion of Norwegian jazz. A sense of fun permeates the record, which has an infectious energy (Sauajazz, September 4). Also hailing from Norway, Hans P. Kjorstad finds room for jazz, folk, rock, modern composition and more in the welcoming Inn. An intriguing quirk of the “miniature orchestra” ~ each of the track titles has three letters (Phantom Limb, September 18).   Hypergarden‘s self-titled debut is a series of freeform jams bordering on rock. Our favorite title is “Invasion of the Hydrangeas” (September 25). The improvising trio Lothar Ohlmeier / Isambard Khroustaliov / Rudi Fischerlehner unveils Landscapes on October 9, referencing both musique concrète and punk (Not Applicable). Mike Reed’s Separatist Party is rocking and rolling on Sing the Color Blue, another left turn from the always reliable Thrill Jockey (October 22). Between avant jazz and noise lies the raucous Evangelium, from Frode Gjerstad / Karl Bjorå / Håvard Skaset. The music tumbles, intertwines and roars (Conradsound, October 1). Eyes of Moon is a loud, romping jam from Tomchess, a multi-instrumentalist joined by a cavalcade of stars (Amalgam, September 15). The iconoclastic Ka Baird teams with Chris Ryan Williams to present Enthalpy. Onomatopoeic vocals are laid atop diagonal instrumentation, sounding like curious creatures from another world (Outside Time, September 25). Richard Allen

items.body: Jamaican singer and songwriter Protoje filmed part of the video for “1000 Lashes” inside the Adwa Victory Memorial Museum in Addis Ababa, built on the site where Ethiopian forces defeated invading Italian troops in 1896 and kept the country free of colonial rule. Born in Saint Elizabeth and twice nominated for the Best Reggae Album Grammy for A Matter of Time and Third Time’s the Charm, the artist confronts the moral cost of global inequality before turning that inquiry onto his own life. Writing from a position of relative privilege, he weighs his own domestic comfort through the line “I’ve got my blessings and I’m feeling no pain,” before reflecting on generational injustice, exploitation, and child labour once his front door closes. Guest vocalist Stephen Marley sings the chorus, “All the children are ours,” right after Protoje admits his own peace. The next verse lists what that peace costs elsewhere: backs lashed a thousand times, communities broken apart, opportunities stolen, wrongdoing shielded by immunity, and children working mines and sent into conflict. SAMO directed the video across two sites bound up in that history: the museum in Addis Ababa, and the steps of 56 Hope Road in Kingston, the Marley family home turned museum. “1000 Lashes” is extracted from The Art of Acceptance, Protoje’s latest album arrived in April via In.Digg.Nation Collective and Ineffable Records. He plays Ruhr Reggae Summer in Mülheim an der Ruhr and Uprising Festival in Bratislava across the same weekend at the end of August, followed by dates across the United States through September and the Welcome to Jamrock Reggae Cruise in November. You can get your copy of The Art of Acceptance HERE and check out Protoje’s upcoming tour dates The post Daily Discovery: Protoje Ft. Stephen Marley – 1000 Lashes appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Review by Kayhan — Every now and then you come across an album that makes all the usual genre labels feel completelyuseless. For me, betcover!!'s UMA is easily one of the most interesting, downright fun and genuinelystrange records to come out of Japan in recent years. Trying to put a label on it feels prettypointless, if I had to describe it it's simply jazz-rock with no limits.The first thing that grabbed me was the emotional range across the tracklist. In one song you feellike you're losing your mind to frantic rhythms, loud brass and wild energy. Then unexpectedly thenoise drops away, and you hear this quiet, deeply sad melody that cuts straight to the heart. Veryfew bands can pull off that kind of contrast without sounding messy or broken.Importantly, none of the intricate parts feel like showing off for the sake of it. The jazz turns,the prog patterns and the odd experiments blend together so naturally that the music always feelsalive and unpredictable, never sterile.It packs intense energy, complex ideas and deep sadness all into a single spin. That balance isessentially why I love both prog and jazz in the first place. It's not about cold technicalperfection, but the thrill of unpredictability and the actual emotional weight behind every note.Also, do yourself a favor and check out their live performances if you get the chance. The songstake on a completely different life on stage and the raw energy makes the whole thing hit evenharder.

items.body: Review by Kayhan — Messa's Close has completely stuck with me lately. It's definitely one of the freshest things I'veheard in the genre, mostly because hearing a doom metal band fold Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, andNorth African motifs into their sound without turning it into a cheap gimmick is pretty rare. Theybalance the thick, crushed doom riffs with loose stoner vibes really well, never losing that moodyatmosphere.The jazz phrasing and soulful guitar work give the record a lot of personality, especially whenpaired with traditional acoustic instruments like the oud. The tracklist takes a couple of sharpdetours, too. You get "Hollow," which is this quiet, eerie acoustic breather, and then right aroundthe corner is "Leffotrak"?a 45-second blast of raw, screamed aggression. On paper, it shouldn'twork, but it never actually breaks the album's flow.The real anchor here, though, is Sara Bianchin. Her voice is remarkably clean and subtle, avoidingany over-the-top dramatics, but it carries a quiet emotional weight that pulls you right into thetracks.Trackwise, "Pilgrim" is easily the highlight for me especially that acoustic build that detonatesinto a wall of heavy riffs. "Rubedo" has a killer solo, while "Serving Him" and "If You Want Her toBe Taken" hold up just as well. Solid, weird, and deeply rewarding listen from front to back.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — A Dark Poem, Part III: The Messiah Complex by Green Carnation is a nice ending to the trilogy of albums they've released since last year, but compared to the first 2, it isn't as gripping or spectacular. With only 3 songs, along with a long orchestral suite that almost acts like the trilogy's end credits, the songs just aren't as strong compared to the outstanding material on the first 2 parts. But besides that, the overall musicianship is outstanding, with great mixes of gothic, progressive, folk and doom metal, and vocalist Kjetil Nordhus giving an impressive diverse performance, proving again that he's one of metal's most underlooked gems. I'd give this a high 6 to low 7 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is The Messiah Complex.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 985"The Ten Legendary Singles" is a compilation of Led Zeppelin and was released in 1989. As the title suggests, it compiles the ten first and most successful singles released by the group on their entire career, including its respective B sides. It has songs from all their eighth studio albums plus a song that was only released on the compilation "Coda"."The Ten Legendary Singles" is a package with an easy to open box set with picture sleeves, a book focusing on the singles released and with a cover with a substantial painting. It was released with a very limited distribution before being discontinued. So, there's a good reason that very few have ever heard of this release and few have a copy of it."The Ten Legendary Singles" has twenty tracks. "Good Times Bad Times" and "Communication Breakdown" are from "Led Zeppelin". "Good Times Bad Times" is the A side and "Communication Breakdown" is the B side. "Good Times Bad Times" is a powerful rock song with nice riffs and a great vocal work with excellent chorus. "Communication Breakdown" is a powerful rock song with a great guitar riff. "Living Loving Maid (She's Just A Woman)" and "Whole Lotta Love" are from "Led Zeppelin II". "Whole Lotta Love" is the A side and "Living Loving Maid (She's Just A Woman)" is the B side. "Living Loving Maid (She's Just A Woman)" is a short catchy song with a nice guitar riff and a good vocal work. "Whole Lotta Love" is a song basically driven by a simple and typical but effective guitar riff of Page. "Immigrant Song" is from "Led Zeppelin III" and "Hey, Hey, What Can I Do" is a non-album's song. It was recorded, as a bonus track, on "Coda". "Immigrant Song" is the A side and "Hey, Hey, What Can I Do" is the B side. "Immigrant Song" is a very short track with a very fast tempo beat. "Hey Hey, What Can I Do" is an acoustic nice ballad, a bluesy rock piece. It's not great but it's not bad either. "Black Dog Man" and "Misty Mountain Hope" are from "Led Zeppelin IV". "Black Dog Man" is the A side and "Misty Mountain Hope" is the B side. "Black Dog" is a great and powerful song with a blues/rock riff and where Plant has one of his best vocal performances. "Misty Mountain Hop" is a great song that represents a good rock moment but isn't as good as most of the songs on that album. "Rock And Roll" and "Four Sticks" are from "Led Zeppelin IV" too. "Rock And Roll" is the A side and "Four Sticks" is the B side. "Rock And Roll" is a fantastic straight typical Rock'n'Roll number with a great drumming work and a nice guitar work. "Four Sticks", like "Misty Mountain Hop", is also a great song, but hasn't the same quality level of the most of the songs on that album. "Over The Hills And Far Away" and "Dancing Days" are from "Houses Of The Holy". "Over The Hills And Far Away" is the A side and "Dancing Days" is the B side. "Over The Hills And Far Away" has a great acoustic guitar performance by Page. It's an interesting song that mixes the beautiful acoustic ballad with the hard rock. "Dancing Days" is one of the most commercial songs on that album. It's good, but less good than some of the songs on that album. "The Crunge" and "D'yer Ma'ker" are from "Houses Of The Holy" too. "D'yer Ma'ker" is the A side and "The Crunge" is the B side. "The Crunge" is a funky song, a tribute to James Brown. I never liked particularly of this song really. "D'yer Mak'er" is a song influenced by reggae. It isn't a bad song but it's out of the context of that album. "Trampled Under Foot" and "Black Country Woman" are from "Physical Graffiti". "Trampled Under Foot" is the A side and "Black Country Woman" is the B side. "Trampled Under Foot" is a kind of catchy song with relatively complex arrangements especially on Page's guitar effects and riffs. "Black Country Woman" is an acoustic blues 517song. It's a typical folk song with good vocals and pounding drumming. "Royal Orleans" and "Candy Store Rock" are from "Presence". "Candy Store Rock" is the A side and "Royal Orleans" is the B side. "Royal Orleans" is a funky influenced song with a nice drumming performance on it. "Candy Store Rock" is a monotonous boring song. Like "Royal Orleans", it's a weak song for Led Zeppelin. "Fool In The Rain" and "Hot Dog" are from "In Through The Out Door". "Fool In The Rain" is the A side and "Hot Dog" is the B side. "Fool In The Rain" is a song dominated by piano with a Latin touch. It spans several genres with a surprising samba section. "Hot Dog" is influenced by country music. I don't like particularly of this kind of music.Conclusion: "The Ten Legendary Singles" is a strange and special compilation album from Led Zeppelin. For those, like me, who have all the ten studio albums from the band, we may say this is probably an item with little interest. In reality, it has only one track that we can't get on their official studio discography, "Hey, Hey, What Can I Do". So, we can ask, who is interested in a compilation like this? In my humble opinion, there's only one kind of person that can be hardly interested in it, the most diehard fans of the band. I've no doubt in saying this is a real blessing for those who can purchase a rare gem like this. Still, despite the good quality, I'm sure this isn't a great item that is worth hunting, especially because it's a very fairly impracticable purchase and very expensive to get it, if that's possible. So, according to what I said before, "The Ten Legendary Singles" is a good addition, but only to any collector fan of Led Zeppelin.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by alainPP — A 13th EP, serving as a prelude to the full CD release later this year. It features diverse influences?progressive rock, classical, and electronic?with echoes of Pink Floyd, Marillion, Steven Wilson, and other British acts."Smile, Smile, Smile," which will appear on the upcoming CD, offers a technical, electro-crossover sound; musically, it flirts with the work of Steven Wilson and Brian Eno, while the lyrics draw inspiration from Philip K. Dick. The sound is designed to reflect the protagonist's disorientation, creating an atmosphere that is latent, schizoid, and oppressive."The Amber Hour"?the first of two instrumental tracks?is gentle, atmospheric, and jazzy, featuring shimmering guitar work. Its sound leans toward Gilmour-esque and Floydian territory, characterized by melting guitar tones and enveloping synths."Broken Arrow" is more experimental and eclectic, driven by wild, seemingly untamable synths. It features a frenetic pace and a swirling melody reminiscent of the 80s and 90s?the previous millennium?while also offering a fresh, punchy pop-crossover vibe.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are very special live albums that, despite not featuring new studio material, innovate through their arrangements or live performances. This gives them a unique quality, one just as valuable as that of conventional studio productions.Renaissance's live album at Carnegie Hall is special for many reasons. No other band integrated an orchestra into its compositional and performance dynamics quite like Renaissance; indeed, the New York Philharmonic acts as an additional member of the group. The performances by John Tout on piano and Jon Camp on bass are superb, particularly because they improvise and venture beyond the familiar versions of the songs (the true hallmark of a great live album, and what gives it a life of its own). And finally, there is Annie Haslam, the star and heart of the group, whose voice (exquisite and pristine) guided both band and audience safely home, much like the sirens' song to Ulysses, though in this instance, leading them in the right direction."Prologue", which was on the first album featuring Annie in the band, was always one of my favorite tracks: its opening, evoking Chopin's "Revolutionary" Etude, followed by that jazz-style fugue. Annie doesn't sing; instead, she follows the melody with her voice, and nothing more is needed. "Can You Understand" is another track that packs a punch live; the piano and bass exude confidence, and when the clavinet joins in, a whole new dimension comes into play. The song is from Ashes Are Burning, another of the band's classic albums. Here, the clavinet sounds deeper and more pronounced, making the gateway to another realm, into which the quintet always transports us, feel all the more immediate. The orchestra is also present, and the moments with an Oriental flavor sound enigmatic and emotionally dark, more so than ever before."Running Hard" is from one of my favorite albums, Turn of the Cards, actually the first one I ever Heard, and its piano introduction sounds just as breathtaking live as the original; it embodies not only Romanticism but also Impressionism. The introduction to "Mother Russia" is also noticeably different from the familiar version, featuring a very delicate piano section, followed by a passage enhanced by the power of the live orchestra.Jon Camp shares a bit of the history of "Song of Scheherazade" with the audience before the performance begins; the bass work shines, and the orchestra truly comes into its own, weaving together Arabian and Eastern motifs with Spaghetti Western elements reminiscent of Ennio Morricone. The choir rivals the power of Pink Floyd's Atom Heart Mother in its grandeur and sonic impact. The vocal sections and central melody are every bit as perfect and wonderful as the familiar ones, and the voices of Annie and Jon blend ideally in their duet. The orchestra's trombones and horns seem to float in the air as Annie's voice soars even higher... and what is there to say? Every time you hear it, it feels like the very first time."Ashes Are Burning" expands from eleven minutes to nearly twenty-four, featuring new improvisational sections where the bass, drums, and piano trio truly shine. Once again, the clavinet is brought prominently to the fore, followed by a jazz-infused section with impeccable timing and a passionate bass solo that maintains the tension throughout, creating the feeling of actually being there with the band.The album was released at a pivotal momento, 1976, crowning the band's golden era, during which they pushed the possibilities of the very style they had created to the limit. I am sure the performance benefited because the band fed off the audience's energy, that unique communion that can only happen at live shows.

items.body: Mozart completed the Clarinet Concerto in October 1791, less than two months before his death, for his friend Anton Stadler. Writing to his wife from Prague that month, he reported that he had nearly finished scoring the finale. Stadler most likely gave the first performance in Prague a few days later, though no program from the concert survives. It was the last concerto Mozart finished, and the autograph has been lost. All that remains in his hand is an earlier sketch of the first movement, written for basset horn. Stadler played a basset clarinet, which reached four semitones below the standard instrument, and Mozart used that extra depth. When the concerto was first published in 1801, the solo part was rewritten for the ordinary clarinet in A. That version held the stage for a century and a half. The orchestra is small: strings, two flutes, two bassoons and two horns, with no oboes, so the wind color sits high and light around the soloist. The three movements run from a spacious Allegro through a long-breathed Adagio to a Rondo finale. Recordings now divide between the familiar 1801 text and reconstructions of the basset original, and that choice shapes both the tone and the reach of the solo line. Here are The Classic Review editorial team’s recommendations for the best recordings of Mozart’s Clarinet Concerto. Thea King, English Chamber Orchestra, Jeffrey Tate Thea King’s 1985 recording did more than any other to make the basset clarinet a working choice for this concerto. It remains the yardstick for everyone who has played it that way since. Her phrasing is the first thing you notice. Long lines are broken into small, searching units, each given its own shape, yet nothing sounds fussy. She plays a modern-system instrument and uses the reconstructed solo part with adjustments of her own. Lyrical breadth sits beside darker, more shaded moments, and she gives full weight to the loud passages when the music asks for it. In the Adagio she draws on the cooler upper register to touching effect and leads back to the theme with a short, unforced cadenza. The finale signs off with a wink, a dive to the bottom of the range and a trill. Jeffrey Tate and the English Chamber Orchestra play with clarity and poise, and the Clarinet Quintet completes the disc. Next to the recordings that followed, hers is the broader, more traditional one, and for many that is exactly its appeal. King Amazon Presto Apple Jack Brymer, London Symphony Orchestra, Colin Davis Where King builds the line from its details, Jack Brymer sings it whole. This 1964 recording with Colin Davis and the London Symphony Orchestra is the classic account of the concerto on the ordinary clarinet, in the text most people grew up with. Davis keeps the orchestra alert, with a lift in the rhythm and plenty of drive, always held in elegant check. Brymer’s tone is gentle and sustained, with a warm glow around every note, and his manner has an unhurried grace that belongs to an earlier age of playing. He never loses the shape of the long phrase. Tempos are quicker than in the most spacious versions of the piece, which makes the outer movements more exciting and a little less consoling. The Allegri Quartet joins him for the Clarinet Quintet. Listeners who want the concerto as they know it from the concert hall, without the extra low notes, should start here. Brymer Amazon Presto Apple Martin Fröst, Amsterdam Sinfonietta, Peter Oundjian The quietest playing on this list is here. Martin Fröst, recorded in 2002 with the Amsterdam Sinfonietta under Peter Oundjian, controls dynamics down to a whisper, and those pianissimos are the memory the disc leaves behind. The Adagio is the heart of the performance, inward without turning solemn, shaped as one unbroken arc. He makes the most of the contrast between the high and low voices of his instrument, whose bottom register is dark and smoky. The outer movements are buoyant and nimble, with a springy opening. The accompaniment is refined and well balanced, and the Vertavo Quartet joins Fröst for the Clarinet Quintet. The result can seem cool precisely because it is so immaculate, and one or two of the whispered passages sound overdone. If the slow movement is what you listen for, this is the version to hear. Fröst Amazon Presto Apple Sabine Meyer, Staatskapelle Dresden, Hans Vonk Sabine Meyer and Hans Vonk sound like partners here rather than soloist and accompanist. Their 1990 recording with the Staatskapelle Dresden pairs exuberance with poignancy, and it has a confident directness. Where Fröst turns inward, Meyer is outgoing, and Vonk matches her with an orchestra that has life in it from the opening to the last bar. She takes the long descending runs of the first movement with complete control, and moves between detached and slurred notes without a seam. Her tone is deeper and rounder than the ordinary clarinet’s, and it stays even from top to bottom. The Sinfonia Concertante for winds fills out the disc. Anyone who prizes the slower, more majestic manner of the classic readings may want more repose than she offers. The pacing is close to Brymer and Davis, and the result stands fully beside them. Meyer Amazon Presto Apple Antony Pay, Academy of Ancient Music, Christopher Hogwood Antony Pay plays a modern copy of a period basset clarinet, and Christopher Hogwood’s Academy of Ancient Music matches him with instruments of Mozart’s time. Recorded in 1984, this is the historically minded choice here, and it is bold, energetic and dance-like. Every phrase is articulated with personality, his added decoration is tasteful, and the Rondo goes with a thrilling ease. The old-style clarinet has a reedy, liquid sound that sets it apart at once from the familiar tone, and he colors it softly and naturally. Hogwood drives the tuttis with spirit and leaves the soft passages open and uncluttered. Later recordings of this historical kind bring more nuance, and this one stays plainer and simpler. The Oboe Concerto, with Michel Piguet, makes the coupling. Choose it if you want the concerto as its first audience might have heard it, ornaments and all. items.artist: Vancouver Post-Punk Quartet Actors Release New Album “Our Love Will Live Forever”

items.body: Between the teeth of misery The hunger takes a hold of me I take my time now I make it right now ACTORS have always sounded like they knew that the nightclub was going to get closed down by gentrification eventually, which may explain why their new album Our Love Will Live Forever hits with such peculiar force: this time the closing hour has stopped being metaphor, and now indeed is the time to party like there is no tomorrow, because tomorrow is never guaranteed. Mastermind Jason Corbett suffered a serious cardiac emergency while making the record, and suddenly all those polished guitars, black-glass synthesizers, romantic fixations, and doomed little dances had to answer to the wails of an ambulance. “Getting wheeled into an emergency room and spending days in the cardiac care unit put me in a state of deep reflection,” Corbett reflects. “Would I finish the album? Would I ever be on a stage again? I was given a second chance to cherish every experience and live in the moment. My goal was to bring that energy to the album.” You can hear it. These songs carry the nervous velocity of somebody who has seen the trapdoor beneath ordinary life and decided to dance directly over it. The title predates Corbett’s hospitalization. Our Love Will Live Forever is engraved on his grandparents’ tombstone, which already carried enough emotional freight before Death suddenly walked into the studio and pulled up a chair. Afterward, the words became a dare…if everybody knows this grim appointment is coming, then what are you doing with the hours beforehand? Left On Read is a beautifully petty modern nightmare, romance reduced to glowing glass, silence, and the humiliating authority of an unanswered message. Corbett turns digital abandonment into old-fashioned psychic damage while the band dresses the anxiety in immaculate synths and guitars. Once upon a time heartbreak required somebody to slam a door. Now your phone can ruin an entire evening without making a sound. Then CTRL starts issuing orders. Its hook has the merciless efficiency of advertising copy, the rhythm grabs the hips before permission has been granted, and guitar lines cut across the synths with sudden flashes of attitude. Depeche Mode’s leather poise, the Human League’s pop nerve, Bootblacks, and the exploratory rush of early Simple Minds can all be detected in the bloodline, but ACTORS have been doing this too long to sound like record collectors arranging their shelves. “(CTRL) is a rally cry, a reaction to a world spinning out of control,” says Corbett. “Being true to yourself is an act of resistance.” That sentence could have come off a placard. On the record, it becomes physical. Elsewhere, memory, desire, fear, and attachment keep colliding without turning the album into some tasteful meditation on mortality suitable for soft lighting and solemn nodding. Corbett’s production at Jacknife Sound stays beautifully controlled while allowing plenty of abrasion around the edges. Drums land with authority, basslines keep the blood moving, guitars carve openings through the synths, and his voice maintains that familiar balance between romantic composure and somebody quietly coming apart behind it. By album three, ACTORS have nothing left to prove about belonging to post-punk. Our Love Will Live Forever is after a nastier question: what happens when mortality quits being philosophy and becomes paperwork, hospital lights, machines, and the possibility that your unfinished record stays unfinished? Their answer makes excellent sense. Turn it up while you still can. Our Love Will Live Forever is out now via Artoffact Records, on vinyl, CD, and all major digital and streaming platforms. Listen to the album below and order it here. Our Love Will Live Forever by ACTORS ACTORS go on tour throughout Europe and Canada this autumn! The tour takes ACTORS across Europe in September, with stops in Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Spain, France, and the UK before heading back to Canada in October. The run includes festival appearances, club shows, and a closing stretch through Vancouver, Edmonton, and Calgary. items.album: Illinois Post-Punk Quartet The House Flies Share Video for “Derelict Crawl”
items.excerpt: Folded arms to rest drinking tea and farmer’s mist Away away don’t crawl away derelict summer and spaces kissed Sew down the spring with needles and grins Slip slip and quietly slip through cracks in all our limbs The House Flies make music for rooms where the wallpaper has started to peel, and nobody has bothered to ask what is growing underneath. items.body: Folded arms to rest drinking tea and farmer’s mist Away away don’t crawl away derelict summer and spaces kissed Sew down the spring with needles and grins Slip slip and quietly slip through cracks in all our limbs The House Flies make music for rooms where the wallpaper has started to peel, and nobody has bothered to ask what is growing underneath. On Derelict Crawl, the Moline, Illinois quartet drags post-punk through damp timber, rural vacancy, and a low electrical hum, then lets the guitars swell until the song feels too large for the walls holding it. There is familiar DNA in their sound: The Cure’s spacious ache, Joy Division’s repetition, Bauhaus at their most severe – but the band keeps grinding those references into something rougher and more physical. Alex Riggen’s vocal delivery carries a tired, almost narcotized calm while Burnie Eckhardt’s guitar pushes against him in broad, abrasive layers. Ozzie Woods and Nick Pompou hold the center with a rhythm section that understands the usefulness of restraint; the song keeps moving without rushing toward payoff, allowing repetition to become pressure. By the time the refrain returns again, alienation has become less an idea than a condition of the body. That approach suits lyrics full of skin, boiled leather, curled material, needles, tea, bone, and limbs splitting open at the seams. Domestic life gets strange fast, with ordinary objects contaminated by private meaning, as though somebody stayed awake too long in an old farmhouse and began assigning motives to everything in the kitchen. The recurring disconnection gives the song its ugly little heartbeat: people trying to remain near each other while every image suggests contraction, damage, or escape. “‘We kept coming back to this one as the first song to release and show a glimpse into the new album,” says vocalist and guitarist Alex Riggen. “It has some of the record’s weight and repetition without giving away too much of what comes later.” The video keeps the mystery intact, placing the band in silhouette while strange superimposed forms slide across the frame. Its near-psychedelic treatment suits a song already interested in warped perception, repetition, and bodies becoming unfamiliar to themselves. “Derelict Crawl works more through images and repetition than a clear narrative, and we like leaving room for people to decide what it means to them. ‘We don’t belong’ is probably as close as the song gets to giving away its center. We approached the video the same way. It creates its own strange little environment without trying to explain the lyrics.” Watch the video for Derelict Crawl below: As the first glimpse of the seven-track Lions and Ore, due November 6, Derelict Crawl suggests The House Flies have learned how much menace can live inside patience. The band stretches its post-punk foundation toward shoegaze weight and gothic rock austerity, leaving enough empty space for every guitar surge to feel earned. Those hundred black vinyl copies may end up carrying one impressively diseased little document of Midwestern isolation. Pre-order the album here. On Friday, November 6, 2026, the band will celebrate the album release at Raccoon Motel, Davenport, IA, with King of the Weirdos, Company Dimes, and Half Loves. items.body: I will be there in a vintage Mugler negligee come and go, take your troubles away… Viva l’amore! Long live love, without pain. Everybody knows the bargain is impossible, which makes singing it feel deliciously reckless. What began as words for one lover has widened into a hymn for appetite, where pleasure becomes moral, beauty practically compulsory. Sweet Love Under Tyranny has a name that sounds ready to be painted across the side of a limousine headed for a disco or a minor apocalypse, and Viva L’Amore, the second track from the project’s forthcoming self-titled EP, carries itself with the same expensive nerve. The Los Angeles producer and vocalist takes darkwave, gothic pop, and the synthetic romance of Italo disco, then stuffs them into a song concerned with the oldest bad idea in civilization: that love might be separated from pain. The song lives on movement. A Synclavier bass strum enters the hook with enough physical authority to make stillness seem impolite, while Matia Simovich’s co-production keeps the arrangement spacious enough for every drum hit, synth accent, and vocal turn to register. Lilian Void’s solo adds a flash of virtuosity without turning the record into a showroom, and Josh Bonati’s mastering preserves the dynamics rather than crushing everything into one gleaming rectangle. There is luxury everywhere, although the luxury has teeth. This quality suits the lyric, which imagines midnight desire as temporary exile from consequence: champagne, sea air, vintage Mugler, secret rooms outside ordinary time. Sweet Love Under Tyranny explains its origin with equal appetite: “It’s about a quickening all of the truly good and beautiful things in life: love, food, sex… silk chiffon… the end of summer just before fall… the real reasons for living! The hook wafted into my consciousness after a family trip to Sicily when the salt was still fresh on my skin from the sea, and I was full of wine, and pasta, and life from the spirit of the place. Initially it was just “Viva l’amore” repeated on the hook, but my friend Mayumi suggested I alternate with senza dolore, which of course, was precisely the move.” Listen to Viva L’Amore and pre-order the Sweet Love Under Tyranny EP here. Sweet Love Under Tyranny EP by Sweet Love Under Tyranny Viva L’Amore also sharpens the promise of Sweet Love Under Tyranny’s self-titled EP, due November 6 via à La Carte Records on digital formats and, for the first time, vinyl. Clear and two-tone black-in-clear editions suit music this obsessed with surfaces, sensation, and presentation. Beneath all that elegance sits a blunt proposition: life is brief, the bottle is open, desire is present, and somebody had better dance. items.body: Where’s the joy in this all? Where’s the light in the dark My hands hide my tears, I feel so lost This first day of Fall Summer does not end so much as loosen its grip. The green world, having spent itself extravagantly, begins to remember that fullness and disappearance are partners. Leaves turn because life is not obliged to remain at its brightest. The air cools, light lowers, and what seemed permanent reveals itself as a passing arrangement. Autumn teaches without speaking: beauty depends upon change, and change upon loss. Yet nothing is truly lost; forms simply withdraw into other forms. The falling leaf is not a failure of the tree, but part of its rhythm. So too, perhaps, are we, within nature’s larger turning. Despair can still dance. Since forming in Los Angeles in 2021, DECEITS (Kevin Moreno and Francisco Saenz) have dragged the music back toward blood, romance, and movement, pulling from the Spanish-language records that surrounded them growing up and letting those rhythms rub against basslines built for dark rooms. The First Day Of Fall comes from a worse place. Moreno wrote it the day before his birthday, during a morning when the approaching occasion felt less like celebration than accusation. Birthdays carry the ridiculous expectation that happiness should report for duty on schedule, and the song turns that pressure inside out. Here is somebody staring at another year of existence and wondering whether disappearance might be easier. When Moreno sings, “I dream to be forgot,” the line lands with the ugly simplicity of a thought you wish you had never admitted to yourself. The music, meanwhile, moves with enough force to keep despair from becoming static. Bass sits at the center with a cold, muscular authority, pushing against a hard drum pattern while guitars spread reverb across the track in broad, abrasive sheets. Gothic synthesizers hang behind the rhythm section, giving the song a sense of scale without smothering its punk impulse. There is a useful contradiction in hearing music this alive carrying words preoccupied with erasure, as though the body has decided to keep moving even while the mind is filing objections. Moreno’s voice makes that conflict sharper. In the quieter passages he bends into a soft, almost romantic delivery, letting the words hover close to the ear before climbing toward a piercing upper register when the arrangement surges. The shift feels less theatrical than involuntary, like restraint finally losing the argument. The production owes an obvious debt to the cavernous records of the 1980s gothic underground, though the mix has enough present-day weight to keep the references from turning archival. Reverb creates depth around the guitars and vocals, but the bass and drums remain immediate, physical, and slightly dangerous. Every element seems placed to preserve tension rather than polish it away. Listen to The First Day of Fall below: The First Day of Fall turns a private crisis into forward motion, carrying self-erasure, birthday dread, and the changing season inside a rhythm section that keeps pressing ahead. With the Hurt As Much As Me Tour 2026 on the horizon, DECEITS sound ready to take that contradiction straight into the room, where pain becomes volume and motion becomes temporary proof of life. Maybe that is DECEITS’ gift: making anguish feel communal without sanding down its teeth. Listen to The First Day of Fall below and order the single here. items.body: Stumbling down the walk of fame Amanda Bynes is on my brain Just wrote a letter to Josephine She’s the girl who stole my dopamine Desire is a rotten eyewitness. Give it enough darkness, dopamine, and unfinished business, and it will swear that the same face is waiting in every crowd. At three in the morning, recognition can become a confidence trick: a familiar cut of hair across the room, a profile caught beneath club lights, a stranger briefly assigned the identity of the person occupying your thoughts. The eyes supply fragments; obsession fills in the rest. Los Angeles musician Andreas Emmanuel drags that perceptual error onto the dance floor in Hallucinations, the latest single from Sun Spoiler. Following Reek, his 101-second account of lovebombing, ghosting, and digital self-abasement, the new track returns to what he calls “delusional hyperfixation.” This time, romantic fixation has passed through the screen and begun altering the visible world. Every blonde in Hollywood becomes a suspect, memory starts impersonating sight, and the brain sends its face-recognition machinery into catastrophic overdrive. “If you’ve ever had someone on the top of your mind you might be able to relate to the experience of thinking you see them everywhere you go, even if they’re not really there,” says Emmanuel. “I recently had this happen to me at a dimly lit nightclub in Hollywood at 3am. I still to this day have no idea if the person I thought I saw was really there, or if it was just another blonde girl, or even if it was Amanda Bynes, who I also seem to see everywhere I go in my neighborhood. It didn’t help that I was wearing a single colored eye contact that made it really tough to see.” The song opens on a quirky, faintly giallo-esque synth-pop figure as a rhythmic bass line begins tightening the screws. Emmanuel enters in a low, smoke-dark register with an ’80s glamrock meets Electroclash, delivering each line with enough bounce to make the unraveling feel recreational. Guitar accents cut across the arrangement in brief, bright angles while synth-pop, darkwave, and dark indie pop squeeze into the same narrow corridor. The chorus breaks open around the cry of “Woah! hallucinating,” a splendidly direct hook that turns psychic disarray into something a crowded room can shout back. Then there is the key change, arriving near the end like another dose administered just as the fixation should be wearing off. The lift pushes the final chorus further into delirium, tilting the floor beneath a song that has carried a funhouse-mirror distortion from its first synth notes. Emmanuel keeps the arrangement lean, allowing the hook, bass, and vocal attitude to do the heavy work. The lyric’s sharpest joke places Napoleon beside Amanda Bynes, binding imperial history and Hollywood disorientation with the rhyme of “Josephine” and “dopamine.” Emmanuel explains: “I try to include a line about a mythological, historical or fantasy figure in each of my songs, and this one is particularly potent in referencing Napoleon’s letters to Josephine. It really struck me that the powerful alpha-male emperor of Europe was essentially a simp for his wife Josephine.” That collapse of self-respect lends Hallucinations much of its clever humor. In Emmanuel’s vision, the once-commanding military man transforms into a frantic correspondent, craving affection to regain his balance. “I see her face when I sleep / I see her face when I dream” propels the obsession through every ounce of consciousness before “I’m just a dog looking for a meal” snatches away the last shred of imperial dignity. Hallucinations occupies the uneasy territory where a person can recognize his own absurdity without escaping it. “You say I’m crazy well yeah I know” functions as a confession, a punchline, and a singalong; self-awareness watches from the passenger seat while compulsion drives. Funny, lean, and catchy as hell, the track gathers a questionable nightclub sighting, one obstructed eye, Napoleon’s letters, and an Amanda Bynes apparition into a compact dark-pop spiral. Self-produced by Emmanuel and mastered by Carl Saff, Hallucinations is out now. Listen to Hallucinations below, or via the streaming service of your choice, and order the single here. items.body: Bourbon has ruined romances, started fistfights, improved lies, destroyed judgement, and convinced generations of perfectly reasonable people that singing at 2:17 in the morning was an excellent idea. Los Tres Mortales understand its dramatic possibilities: their debut single, Bourbon, throws Caroline Blind and CWHK of Sunshine Blind together with Troy Payne of The Wake, three veterans of American gothic rock who could easily have made something stately and respectable. Thank God they went for the saloon instead. The lyrics leave busted bottles, motel sheets, gasoline, libation-drenched lies, and poor decisions scattered around. The song narrates the story of Blackout Bourbon Baby staggering through this chaos, laughing and smashing whatever’s left to prevent morning from revealing anything. Somewhere between downtown and oblivion, two people continue dancing because sobriety would end the argument forever. CWHK builds the track around drums that hit with blunt purpose and guitars carrying enough weight to make the floorboards complain. Payne steps into the song sounding tightly wound, severe, possibly one drink away from delivering a lecture nobody requested. Then Blind answers him. Her voice brings mischief into the argument, loosening his collar one button at a time while the two circle the fictional Blackout Bourbon Baby from opposite sides. “CWHK gave us the music and the title…and Troy came up with the story of the Blackout Bourbon Baby,” says Blind. “I knew it would be perfect to respond to his character by becoming the voice of the Bourbon Baby herself, telling him to chill out and stop being so tight-laced. The back and forth between two people trying to convince each other of their point of view creates a tension you just don’t get from a single voice. It’s also only somewhat reflective of my actual friendship with Troy!” That “somewhat” is doing magnificent work. The pleasure comes from hearing two personalities collide rather than politely alternate. Payne bears down; Blind needles him. One voice wants control, the other keeps opening another bottle. Their exchange gives Bourbon the shape of an argument that became flirtation somewhere around closing time, and will probably become an argument again before breakfast. Rich W tears through the middle with a lead guitar break that adds another streak of poor planning. Los Tres Mortales themselves began almost as casually. “Some people get together with their friends and play board games or have barbecues,” Blind quips. “When we get together, we share whatever music we’re working on, somebody jumps in with an idea, and suddenly we’re all working together. My advice? Write music with your friends. Collaborate. Celebrate. People were doing it for millennia before the internet!” There are worse manifestos. Tintin’s video wisely avoids sophistication. Blind and Payne perform in front of a wall of fire because sometimes a wall of fire is exactly what civilization has been building toward. Flames leap behind them while both singers attack their roles with the delighted seriousness of people who know melodrama becomes much more enjoyable once you stop apologizing for it. The result is funny, theatrical, cheap-looking in the complimentary midnight-movie sense, and perfectly suited to a song named after brown liquor. Watch below: Produced by CWHK and mastered by William Faith, Bourbon carries decades of experience without behaving like anybody has been appointed curator of the past. Los Tres Mortales sound pleased to be here, pleased to be loud, and especially pleased to discover that friendship, guitars, alcohol mythology, and gratuitous fire remain perfectly serviceable reasons to start a band. items.body: Every definition closes off certain possibilities. Naming an experience can help us understand it, but a name can also become a verdict, reducing a person to one fixed account of who they are and what their wounds mean. Human beings are rarely so easy to settle. We contradict ourselves, bear the consequences of our choices, and continue to change even after others believe they understand us. Resistance may begin there: in defending the right to remain complex, unresolved, and unfinished. Berlin post-punk and darkwave mainstays Golden Apes enter that unsettled territory with Resistance, the first single from The Sun Came Up Tremendously, their twelfth studio album, due September 18 through Icy Cold Records. Released today alongside a film written and directed by vocalist Peer Lebrecht, the song treats opposition as an internal friction: the force that keeps identity from hardening into a final shape, even when certainty would be easier. Resistance opens on a resonant guitar figure, answered by a single low keyboard tone. Hi-hats enter with a dry sizzle; Christian Lebrecht’s bass gives the piece forward pressure, while wavering synths and Salomon Bosse’s drums steadily enlarge the frame. Once the heavier guitar figure lands, the track assumes the emotional scale of mid-’80s gothic rock. Peer Lebrecht sings in a deep baritone that stays composed as the arrangement grows dense, and the guitars follow the cadence of his lines with a spring-loaded post-punk lift before thickening between verses. At intervals, the drums loosen into splashes, and the rhythm pulls back, leaving more air around Peer’s euphoric delivery. A clean, melodic guitar solo settles at the center point, almost plain in its design; its calm gives the vocal’s return greater weight. The measured bass, sober guitar tone, and baritone gravity recall Scottish cult band Lowlife, while the surrounding textures remain recognizably Golden Apes. The band describes the song’s central idea in terms of identity, complexity, and damage: “…Maybe that is the actual resistance. Not resistance against an external system, but resistance against final form. Against definition. Against the temptation to trade complexity for peace. Half-damaged instead of neatly resolved. I am the enemy…” Lebrecht’s film, based on a lucid dream by Vito Schneider, transfers that internal struggle to an abandoned clinical ward rendered in sickly greens and exhausted amber. A striped spinning top travels down an empty corridor; barefoot figures in hospital gowns occupy tiled rooms and enact private systems whose purpose never fully declares itself. One scrubs water from a floor into a bucket, another fills a bathtub, one drinks from a metal cup, and another holds an open umbrella beneath a dry ceiling. A solitary player moves grapes across a checkerboard, while a black telephone waits inside a star-lined suitcase. Elsewhere, a reel-to-reel machine runs beside clasped hands, as though recording testimony from a room that has forgotten its questions. Golden Apes perform throughout the ward, each member stationed apart in bathrooms, bare rooms, and passages. High overhead angles flatten bodies into diagrams, while the repetition of circular objects—the spinning top, fruit, reel hubs, and drum heads—turns the building into a machine for processing unresolved thought. In the closing coda, a black-clad figure carries armfuls of hospital gowns into a laundromat and feeds them into a washer. The garments pass through one more cycle, suggesting cleansing, erasure, recurrence, or all three at once. Watch the video for Resistance below: For more than two decades, Golden Apes have moved among post-punk, darkwave, gothic rock, indie rock, and electronic experiment, bringing delicate guitar melodies, driving bass, and Peer Lebrecht’s sonorous voice into a language of their own. The Berlin group has appeared at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party, and Murder of Crows, toured across Europe, the United States, Canada, and Russia, and shared stages with And Also The Trees, The Chameleons, Pink Turns Blue, Clan of Xymox, She Past Away, Whispering Sons, TRAITRS, Then Comes Silence, and A Projection. The Sun Came Up Tremendously follows the band’s 2024 album Our Ashes at the End of the Day. Its ten songs were written between 2024 and 2025, then recorded and produced at Thommy Hein Studios in Berlin from late 2025 into early 2026. Resistance was mixed by Thommy Hein and Peer Lebrecht and mastered by Hein, who also contributes guest guitar. The current Golden Apes lineup comprises Peer Lebrecht on vocals and synths, Maximilian Hennig and Stephan Schönefeld on guitars, Christian Lebrecht on bass, and Salomon Bosse on drums. “…o sun, that healest all distempered vision, thou dost content me so, when thou resolvest, that doubting pleases me no less than knowing!” – Dante Alighieri, Divina Commedia Listen to Resistance below, and pre-order The Sun Came Up Tremendously through Bandcamp. The album arrives September 18 via Icy Cold Records. items.album: Blutengel releases new single and video ‘Afterlife’

items.body: Berlin darkwave and synthpop band Blutengel released the single and video “Afterlife” on 4 September 2026 via Out Of Line Music. The track is the third single from Blutengel’s upcoming studio album, due in early 2027, following “The Devil” in October 2025 and “Schwarzer Engel” in June 2026. “Afterlife” is a slow-building darkwave track built on melancholic, cinematic electronics carried by a steady pulse. The song combines layered synthesizer parts with a melodic hook, moving between an introspective verse structure and a club-ready tempo. The single arrives ahead of Blutengel’s headline appearance at Dark Summer Open Air Vol. 2, at Wasserschloss Klaffenbach in Chemnitz, on 12 September 2026, with Chrom, Destroy Me Again and Ghostbells confirmed as support. Out Of Line Music describes the show as nearing a sellout. About Blutengel Blutengel was formed in Berlin in 1998 by singer Chris Pohl after he left Seelenkrank, and released its debut album, “Child of Glass,” in 1999. Ulrike Goldmann joined as co-vocalist in 2005 and remains in the band alongside Pohl. Blutengel has released its albums through Out Of Line Music, building a chart record in Germany that includes “Monument” (No. 4, 2013), “Omen” (No. 4, 2015), “Leitbild” (No. 4, 2017), “Un:Gott” (No. 2, 2019) and “Erlösung – The Victory of Light” (No. 4, 2021). Its most recent studio album, “Dämonen: Sturm,” was released in February 2025. Blutengel has since issued “The Devil,” “Schwarzer Engel” and now “Afterlife” as singles ahead of a new studio album planned for early 2027.

items.body: Los Angeles punk/EBM trio Purest Form released its EP “RESISTANCE” on Dais Records on 4 September 2026, closing the six-track set with a cover of The Prodigy’s “Breathe,” a song the band has performed live for some time. The EP is Purest Form’s second release and its first for Dais Records, following a self-titled debut EP in 2024. RESISTANCE by Purest Form “RESISTANCE” runs “Animal,” “Break,” “Beyond Terror,” “More,” “Bass Resistance” and “Breathe.” Purest Form is Story Beeson (vocals), Madi Woodward (guitar, programming) and Riley Oikawa-Dahlson (bass), and the trio draws on members’ backgrounds in hardcore bands alongside a shared interest in industrial and techno production. The EP mixes serrated riffs with fractured breakbeats, basslines and heavy feedback, with nods to death metal and acid house, under Beeson’s shouted, anthemic vocals. Recording took place sporadically through 2025, beginning while Beeson was still evacuated from her home during the Los Angeles wildfires. The band built sketches on computer before moving into open-ended sessions with longtime collaborator and producer Andrew Oswald. “A helpful and needed distraction during a pretty bleak year for the world,” said bassist Riley Oikawa-Dahlson. “It became the one thing that felt good to us. We explore some dark headspaces, but it’s also dance music.” Vocalist Story Beeson connected the EP directly to the year’s events in Los Angeles, including the wildfires and ICE activity: “The nature and actions of our country are overwhelming, I can’t get away from the feeling of ‘what can we do to resist this at all costs?’ We have very radical fantasies across the board, making music that isn’t talking about what’s happening right now just feels unimportant to us.” Beeson also described the EP’s title track directly: “Resistance, less of an idea, more of an absolute action that has to be taken.” Purest Form previously shared a video for “Animal,” the EP’s opening track, which Beeson also directed. Side-Line covered the Dais Records signing and the “Animal” video when it was announced. Tour dates for Purest Form Purest Form has the following live dates confirmed: September 11, 2026 – Los Angeles, CA – The Globe Theater, with Fiddlehead and Pity Sex September 12, 2026 – Pioneertown, CA – Thrasher Death Match at Pappy & Harriet’s, with Circle Jerks and Melvins September 18, 2026 – Austin, TX – Cold Waves Festival September 25, 2026 – Chicago, IL – Cold Waves Festival November 14, 2026 – Orange County, CA – Darker Waves Festival About Purest Form Purest Form formed in Los Angeles in 2023, when Madi Woodward and Story Beeson met while working at an independent venue in the city and bonded over a shared interest in underground music. Beeson also performs with Choking on Ash and Vacant Future, Woodward with Fury and Object of Affection, and Oikawa-Dahlson with Roman Candles and Pocketknife. The trio released a self-titled debut EP in 2024, built around heavy, distorted guitar and programmed percussion, and built a live reputation in the Los Angeles underground over the following two years. Purest Form signed to Dais Records in mid-2026 and shared the video for “Animal” ahead of the EP. “RESISTANCE,” released on 4 September 2026, is the band’s second EP and its first release for Dais Records, recorded through 2025 with producer Andrew Oswald and closing with the band’s cover of The Prodigy’s “Breathe.”

items.body: Striped Light, the long-running collaborative project of English musician and producer Benge (Creep Show, Wrangler, John Foxx and the Maths), releases its debut album “For All This Beauty” on 6 November 2026 via MemeTune. The nine-track record of electronic pop gathers a rotating cast of vocalists and co-writers: Hannah Peel, Elizabeth Bernholz of Gazelle Twin, Serafina Steer, Tara Busch of I Speak Machine, Juliana Venter and Sam Genders of Tunng. The album launches today with its first single, “Atoms”, featuring Tara Busch. Watch the video below. Busch performs with Cabaret Voltaire (alongside Benge) on their final US tour this month. Describing the writing session behind “Atoms” and its sibling tracks, she stated: “I dream now that this record was realised when driving through the streets of LA at night, neon flashing by the peripheral of your eye, endless avenues and curtained windows […] I remember the recording session, down in Benge’s studio underneath the streets of Shoreditch.” The songs date back to 2007, when Benge began writing electronic backing tracks and brought in Genders, then of Tunng, to write lyrics over them. Genders recalled the sessions at Benge’s Shoreditch studio: “It was one of my first co-writing jobs and I was super excited to be sitting in this black box room with floor to ceiling vintage synths on every wall, Benge sitting there in a tweed jacket. I would sing melody and lyric ideas until Benge was happy with them and the songs came together really quickly.” Bernholz, who lends vocals to “Foolish,” described the track as a departure into a simpler pop mode. She commented: “This collaboration feels like a time capsule for innocence and nostalgia, made in a very different time and place, when I was trying to carve a very different sound of my own. I loved the chance to make something simple and sweet. Working with Benge’s beautiful, emotional synth arrangements, the song practically wrote itself and my vocals fell into place so naturally.” Steer, who contributed “Echoes” and “Wake Up,” pointed to the creative circle around Benge’s old studio address as the record’s lasting mark on her. She said: “I have really fond memories of making the tracks with Benge at his studio in Coronet Street, Shoreditch. The record for me represents the ‘scene’ of amazing creativity and people around that studio and Benge – something I wasn’t so aware of at the time!” Peel, who appears on “Dive Deep” and “The City,” linked the songs to a version of London that has since disappeared. She added: “It’s amazing how music can evoke such landscapes […] In an era that was less capitalised, no stag do’s or beanies, when artists ran the buildings and possibilities were endless.” The full tracklist (catalog MEME26VA09) runs “Atoms” (feat. Tara Busch), “Foolish” (feat. Elizabeth Bernholz), “Between the Trees” (feat. Tara Busch), “Dive Deep” (feat. Hannah Peel), “Echoes” (feat. Serafina Steer), “Motorcade” (feat. Tara Busch), “The City” (feat. Hannah Peel), “Wake Up” (feat. Serafina Steer) and “Sleep” (feat. Juliana Venter). Additional musicians on the record include bassist Kuma Harada, Minimoog player Max Middleton and guitarist Mike Lindsay of Tunng. The album’s artwork was created by John Foxx, with illustration by Eoin Richardson. For All This Beauty by Striped Light “For All This Beauty” is available to pre-order through Striped Light’s store ahead of its 6 November release. About Striped Light Striped Light is the collaborative pop project of Benge, the professional name of English musician and producer Benjamin David Edwards. Benge built his career from a home studio collecting vintage synthesisers and drum machines, releasing his own instrumental electronic albums from the mid-1990s and founding the label Expanding Records. His base of operations, MemeTune Studios, began life in a complex under the streets of Shoreditch, East London, before relocating to Cornwall, where he now lives and works. Striped Light grew out of Benge’s parallel love of 1970s and 1980s electronic pop. In 2007, working from his Shoreditch studio, he began writing electronic backing tracks and enlisted Sam Genders of Tunng, whom he knew through Genders’ bandmate Mike Lindsay, to write lyrics over them. Over the following years Benge auditioned and recorded versions of the songs with a rotating group of singers he had met and worked with, including Hannah Peel, Elizabeth Bernholz of Gazelle Twin, Serafina Steer, Juliana Venter and Tara Busch of I Speak Machine, several of whom also produced or co-produced their own early records at his studio. In 2011 Benge travelled to Los Angeles to record Busch’s parts in a vintage studio there. Bassist Kuma Harada, Minimoog player Max Middleton and Tunng guitarist Mike Lindsay filled out the arrangements, and John Foxx, with whom Benge would later form John Foxx and the Maths, created the album’s artwork. The Striped Light songs were largely complete by the early 2010s but were set aside as Benge worked through a run of other collaborations, among them John Foxx and the Maths, Wrangler (with Stephen Mallinder of Cabaret Voltaire and Phil Winter of Tunng) and Creep Show (Wrangler with John Grant), alongside his own solo albums and production work. In 2023, at the prompting of his manager Steve Malins, Benge revisited the old mixes and began remixing them at his newly rebuilt MemeTune Studio in Cornwall. That work has become “For All This Beauty,” out 6 November 2026 on MemeTune – a Striped Light album nearly 20 years in the making.

items.body: Canadian-born, Los Angeles-based artist Kontravoid, the recording name of Cameron Findlay, releases his new album “Sound Of The Void” on 2 October 2026 through Artoffact Records. The announcement comes with the new single “Without”, out now, and digital, vinyl and CD pre-orders are open. “Sound Of The Void” is a 10-track album that mixes coldwave, EBM and electro, and marks Kontravoid’s second full-length for Artoffact Records after 2024’s “Detachment.” The tracklist runs “Sound Of The Void,” “Without,” “Mortal,” “Subject,” “Chances,” “Dimension,” “Forever,” “Abandon,” “Returning” and “Phantom.” “Mortal” previously appeared as a standalone single on Artoffact on 30 January 2026. The album was mixed and mastered by Ewan A. Kay, with cover design by Jean Lorenzo, live drum engineering by Daryl Dee and insert photography by Perpetual Mobile. Sound Of The Void by Kontravoid The album is available for pre-order on Bandcamp as a digital download, on clear vinyl and on CD, along with a limited test pressing. The vinyl and CD editions ship around the album’s 2 October 2026 release date. About Kontravoid Kontravoid is the recording name of Cameron Findlay, a Canadian-born musician, drummer and producer based in Los Angeles who performs behind a masked visual identity. Findlay played drums for Crystal Castles in 2007 and 2008 and co-founded and co-wrote for the Toronto synth-pop band Parallels before leaving in 2011. He released Kontravoid’s self-titled debut album on Toronto label Pretty Pretty Records in February 2012, followed by the single “Native State” that July. The single “Undone” followed in 2018 on Berlin’s Fleisch Records, then “Too Deep” in 2019 and “Faceless” in 2021. Findlay has toured with Boy Harsher, ADULT. and Drab Majesty, and has remixed Schwefelgelb, Kris Baha and, most recently, Buzz Kull’s “In The Cut.” Kontravoid signed to Artoffact Records for the album “Detachment,” released 1 March 2024, followed by the “Losing Game Remixes” EP that December and the single “Mortal” on 30 January 2026. In September and October 2026, Findlay co-headlined a North American tour with Buzz Kull. “Sound Of The Void,” out 2 October 2026, is his second full-length for Artoffact Records and his first album since “Detachment.”
