items.body: From dub to industrial and Tanzania to Thailand, from an untitled album by an unnamed artist to a turntable album without records, our Electronic Music Preview has it all! This adventurous slate is bound to appeal to the mind as well as to the body. Site favorites such as Jónsi and Andy Bell appear in surprising categories, while newcomers make their play for the big time. One thing is sure: the dance floors won’t be empty this season. We’re halfway through our Fall Music Preview, with much more to come; our largest installment is set to appear tomorrow! Our cover image comes from Petrels’ Infangthief, covered below. Bonobo is the biggest name on fall’s electronic slate. Fans won’t have long to wait, as Distance in Static is released on September 11. As with previous efforts, the album offers a mix of vocal and instrumental cuts, the bonus being that the vocal tracks are in English, Urdu and Japanese. We’re enamored with lead cut “Drift,” and expect mainstream success (Ninja Tune). The same (safe) prophecy holds true for Chrome Sparks‘s Ball of Light, especially as the producer has roped in Khalid and Jónsi for lead single Sleeper. The languid opener is not representative of the album as a whole; for a more accurate representation, spin the club-friendly title track and then “Pleasure” (Chrome Sounds/AWAL, September 11). Nathan Fake is back, and it didn’t even take that long! The Caldera EP is a follow-up to Evaporator and the Hypercube EP from February and May (InFiné, October 23).   Bibio & Dorian Concept are releasing the expressive Answers, their first collaborate album after years of friendship. The timbres are warm and inviting, perfect for autumn (Warp, October 16). It’s only fair that we mention The Avalanches, though we’re not yet sure if the album is primarily vocal or instrumental; the sample-based Since I Met You is still one of our all-time favorite albums, and we’d love the same to be true for No Bad Memories, out October 16 and preceded by Can’t Get Over Losing You. Another sample-based artist, Odd Nosdam, is releasing a “love letter to the vinyl format.” On Patrol is packed with slow beats, obscure loops, and enthralling grooves: a crate digger’s delight. Bonus points for the cool cover art, seen right (Alien Transistor, October 23).   Is it acid? Is it jazz? Is it ambience? Is it hardcore? Yes ~ Semiratruth‘s S!M is all of these things and more, hopping genres like low fences in a wide field. A lot of ground is covered in twenty-two tracks, not one longer than 3:04 (Sooper, September 25). Space Afrika‘s Quiet Storm is a study in contrasts: featuring segments of ambience, electronics, opera, hip-hop and modern composition. The support cast is massive, each guest contributing a different aspect of a greater story. A spiritual thread runs through the recording, lifting it to a higher level (Dais, September 25). The snails seen on Carmen Villain‘s Memoira are purposeful; the album is one of “deceleration,” with trumpet, clarinet, flute, piano and strings, all filtered through sluggish beats and dub timbres (Smalltown Supersound, September 4). Post Dub Cities is the new concept album from Adriano Zanni, who wanders an unpopulated landscape and finds it rich in sound. The accompanying photos makes it seem less science fiction than recent history (Bronson Recordings, October 2). Soaked in crackle and reverb, Oblique‘s Ghost Dubs is an exercise in tension and mood. Opening single “Low Times” comes with a series of alternate mixes (Pressure, September 25).   Alien Alarms are Tuned to Different Frequencies. The album investigates a wealth of tonalities, uses creative composition to address the modern malaise of distraction. “The machine is much, but it is not everything” (PATCHWORKS, October 2). พังและแพง splits the difference between ambient and electronic on หัดขับรถ, whose title means “Learning to Drive.” The Thai producer calls the sound “dance music for introverts” (September 4). James Gorczyca also straddles the line between genres, adding a bit of modern composition on Weights of this world., whose aural presence is accompanied by a “visual world” (September 2). Les Brown‘s The One After That is the concluding part of a loose trilogy. Punchy rhythms accompany kind patterns, with a slightly cinematic lean (September 22). According to Short Span, it was “important to have Eden Aurelius‘s Entre Nous out for summer.” Close enough, as the album shimmers like the low angle of the ever-sinking sun. The further south one lives, the greater the impact will be (September 17). Supporting our theory that 2026 is The Year of Blue, Emily A. Sprague offers Cyano, drenched in blue synth and voice. There are various ways to procure the bonus tracks, including 7″ and Japanese CD; a limited edition RISO booklet is also available (RVNG Intl., October 2). Belbury Poly returns with his ninth album, Sorcery, a set of nostalgic sci-fi synth, referencing the golden 80s of sight and sound (September 25). Those who miss disco will be enamored with Narcoba‘s Pechersk. The title track could be mistaken for an instrumental by the Pet Shop Boys (Nisantashi, October 2). Loula Yorke seems always to be in a positive mood, and the upbeat nature of her personality shines through her music. Starling Sessons is filled to the gills with synth and exudes a playful tone (Truxalis, September 4).   Here’s something we didn’t expect: Infangthief and Outfangthief, a pair of interlocking albums from old fave Petrels. The drone remains intact, while the beats come hard and fast, reflecting the time spent revisiting and remixing. (Denovali, October 16). Church meets club on Music for Air, as the duo of Gamut Inc uses computer-controlled pipe organ to produce sounds more suited to Saturday night than to Sunday morning. We hold out hope that this music might find its way into a forward-thinking worship service (Karlrecords, October 16). Ride bassist Andy Bell joins harp and synthesizer duo Masal for Common Primitives, a lovely album whose rock tones set it apart from others in this article. The moods shift from placid to encouraging, often within single pieces, as new aspects of the music are turned toward the light (Sonic Cathedral, October 9). Names On Tapes offers Ayin, which celebrates the Jewish concept of “absence as potential,” the seat of creation. Clarinet, guitar and electronics emerge from the void (September 4). Then from nothing we travel to NOWHERE, found “between movement and stillness,” as PHILMS explores the liminal spaces like “That Uninspiring Beige Building” (November 17).   Slow and steady wins the race. Never rising above 121 BPMs, Philipp de Castro‘s Morferna is a lesson in restraint. “Oximoro” even includes a sound like that of a tea kettle, waiting to boil (Fala Nocturna, September 18). Peter Gall‘s Drum Seeds allows the percussion to take center stage, enhanced by synth and keys, producing a sound somewhere between jazz and electronic, with a trance-like veneer (Compost, September 4). Vintage drum machines, live drumming from Valentina Magaletti and sporadic punk-energy vocals make Holy Tongue‘s Basilikum an exciting experience. Lead single “Coca” might fit into an adventurous goth set (AD 93, October 4). One might expect to find Future Sounds of Jazz, Volume 16 in another department, but while the series honors jazz, it falls firmly into the electronic category and features exclusive tracks (Compost, September 18).   opo collects seven years of experiments on 666ridims (2020-2026), using unconventional rhythms, infusing the music with a pan-cultural flavor (Meakusma, September 3). Don’t be fooled by the opening track; Max Kutner‘s The Illustrated Interior veers from rock to glitch to percolation to prog. Infused with a sci-fi sheen, the album sounds as literary as its title (September 16). Sporting a wild cover by Kat Williams Illustrations (shown left), Ørdop Wolkenscheidt‘s concept album Stallmeister Rittich vs. the Machine takes as its starting point the 18th century lost and found poem “The Ballad of Stallmeister Rittich,” and builds a narrative around the hero’s journey: music unfolding like a narrative in verse (October 9). The slightly scary House with a Curse arrives with a silent film video and a sense of fun, the Halloween love child of Andrew Waslylk and Tommy Perman. There’s a haunted story in these grooves, perfect for the midnight hour (Clay Pipe Music, October 16). We’re digging the video for “Plastic Minds / Elastic Machines,” from Jeremiah Chiu‘s Edge Conditions; the frames flash with the percussion, and the presentation is a breath of fresh air (International Anthem, October 9). With “eight prepared turntables, four mixers, no records, six hands,” Institut für Feinmotorik is an outlier. Öd (meaning “barren” or “boring”) is anything but; these are the sounds our turntables hide from us, brought out of the shadows and into the light (Faitiche, October 9). J. Juva‘s loop-based Unclocked uses techniques invented by Steve Reich to set patterns against each other in a miasma of sound. Don’t expect an ambient record; the album is packed with beats and patterns, angular at times yet still suited for adventurous club floors (September 25). Slaylor Moon makes angular, unconventional machine music, “pushing keys, buttons, pads, or wheels.” Crisis Make Up! heads in unexpected directions, but is never random (Maple Death, October 9).   The post-industrial sound of DIKDӔDØR has evolved over time, and now includes drum machines and a power mixer. Their sound continues to be bleak and uncompromising, but now ~ perhaps ironically ~ one can dance to it. The Entertainer is released September 9 on Edelfaul. Also in this vein, A Tomb Full of Stars walks a post-apocalyptic landscape, decorating it with echoed words and the sounds of forgotten melodies, rescued from the ash. 1:When the Reflection Passes is released on Varia September 22. Fresh from Birdsong (made with birds only), Megafauna returns with an immersive, industrial, self-titled album. Voidscan appears on one track, lending the project to an even darker hue (Syrup Moose, September 25). While the music is informed by tragedy, Anthony Baldino‘s CONVEYER bleeds dramatic tension, offering not healing but catharsis, scoring the pain beat by devastating beat (BL_K Noise, September 18). After 17 years, Lauren Bousfield (Nero’s Day at Disneyland) returns to claim her throne. After influencing many splattercore sci-fi IDM artists, she hasn’t lost a step. The Grand Reopening EP drops October 16, preceded by the Mormon-sampling single ØBabylon. Beautifully harsh sounds decorate Cenizas 1era Parte, a broken beats and bass set from Lima’s XR1S, with an industrial sheen (nodo, September 10).   The fact that deep glens opened for Autechre last year opens a window into the artist’s sound. carver is intricate and melodic, while defying expectations of where the beats might land next (September 17). The beats are generous on Roel Funcken‘s Kine 3, spanning the length of a double CD. In an unusual confluence, the artist will be opening for Autechre this year. As the title implies, this is the continuation of a series that gets better with each installment (EC Underground, September 4). Machine Records is the perfect landing place for Foel, whose IDM rhythms are mysterious and dark, a reflection of difficult experiences. Gwasagaru means “scatter-disperse,” which is exactly what these beats do while dancing around a melodic core (September 4).   The clever unknown-untitled offers the double 12″ uu05 on September 18, with information revealed a week later. This way, the house-techno rhythms can be appreciated on their own, with wild speculation as to their origins. While the spelling is different from the epic poem and film, “odissiy,” the closing track on maxolydian‘s altre galassie, is meant to score the end of a journey: one that spans the galaxies and ends up safe at home (September 1). Uplift (Butterfly) is the first taste of Tom VR‘s Don’t Know How Fast I’m Moving Until I Hit Something, an upbeat set inspired by the story of koi ascending waterfalls to become dragons (Heart Somersault, September 9). Never far from our consciousness is Subsist & Faith Disciplines, who already has a trio of releases lined up for fall. First out of the gate is Not Charlie‘s Inconformista, a seemingly oxymoronic “reflective dance floor album” that somehow accomplishes the feat (September 4). Fleet offers Percussions from Space, although one should not be able to hear said percussion while in space (September 25). Sci-fi dance floors will be enamored by Cathopsis‘ Solythode, a voyage into the outer limits of the universe (Component, September 4). JØHRN offers frigid techno on Miles of Silence Between Us, using music as a metaphor for relationships (October 16). Steady, pulsing techno dominates Oscar Mulero‘s Between Two Worlds, the 199th release from Semantica paving the way for a landmark celebration (September 25). The consistently surprising Nyege Nyege Tapes returns with Jay Mitta‘s rapid-fire Kazi Kwanza, which showcases the vivid sound of the Tanzanian underground. Get ready to sweat it out, as the BPMs approach 200 on multiple occasions (September 4). The BPMs of Silvan Strauss may not be quite as fast, but they are still hyperactive; SPRINTING also boasts an international cast, primed to bring the producer’s vision to full fruition (Kabul Fire, September 4). We are really looking forward to fabric presents Max Cooper. The tracklisting blends old favorites with exclusives, along with some surprising entries. Ólafur Arnalds, Future Sound of London, Lusine and a Roly Porter remix of a Cooper track all share space in this upbeat mix (fabric, October 2). Richard Allen

items.body: Primal Forms is quite a propulsive and beautifully elaborated electronic synthedelica effort that will ravish listeners of adventurous music with dancing, then hallucinogenic qualities. The synergy between the two musicians works like magic and with a clear easiness. A refreshing creative impulse to vintage analog electronic devices Primal Forms by Phantom Horse   Never heard about this project before, but as an avid listener/follower of the excellent Umor Rex‘s musical production, I wanted to give it a try. I must say I did right because this German duo embraces, in a very cool and inspiring way, the revival of Cosmic-electronic music in the pure tradition institutionalized by pioneering 70s sound artists such as Paul Baumann or Edgar Froese (Tangerine Dream), Bernd Kistenmacher, Mario Schönwalder, Software, Cosmic Hoffmann, Michael Hoenig et al, and a few materials reissued by the key label Bureau B. What makes this duo original and distinctive is that the two musicians, Ulf Schütte and Niklas Dommaschk, are capable of giving a second breath and a refreshing creative impulse to vintage analog electronic devices (notably modular synth technologies), thanks to hyper-efficient and trance-inducing minimal electronic pieces. Some tracks and their concise mechanical rhythms based on sequencers are reminiscent of a few synth-pop pioneering works. Globally, the compositions deliver an electro-pop ambient dimension enhanced by almost minimal-techno grooves and downtempo beats. Lysergic moments made of obsessional circular motifs and electronic oscillations are quite perceptible in the superb “Focus.” Some refined neo-psychedelic mantras made of vibrant droney chords, repetitive patterns, and melodious counterpoints will really transport the listener to another dimension. The compositions offer a lot of surprises, strangely experimental moments, and a blooming sense of electro-pop music dominated by catchy melodies. In a way, it operates a nice and welcoming synthesis between abstract synth experimentalism and more pulsating, groovy electronica. The album closes with the spacious, inter-sidereal, mellow, elastic, melodious-tinged, and utterly captivating “Umbra-Mechanik,” which closes the album in a brilliant manner. All in all, Primal Forms is quite a propulsive and beautifully elaborated electronic synthedelica effort that will ravish listeners of adventurous music with dancing, then hallucinogenic qualities. The synergy between the two musicians works like magic and with a clear easiness. Quite recommended for fans of neo-space music with a Berlin-style-oriented sound such as Zombi, Sankt Otten, Emeralds… but also more classical acts of the genre like Harmonia, Conrad Schnitzler, or Radio Massacre International. The album is delivered in a beautiful vinyl format, seconded by a digital version. Primal Forms is available on Umor Rex. [Bandcamp] Primal Forms by Phantom HorseThe post Phantom Horse :: Primal Forms (Umor Rex) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.excerpt: The Swedish sound sculptor enters the backrooms with an album of unstable electronic textures united by their uncanny, reality-warping potential It all starts with a burbling texture. The sound is quilted from what appear to be typical ambient tropes: the hum of water and droplets of static pattering against whispering ash. But things are not as they seem. items.body: For the third episode of our Musical Road to WOMEX, we travel not only in place but also in time: back to Saigon before 1975, when GI bars ran fuzzed-out rock and twist alongside Cải Lương theatres and bolero radio. That’s the era Saigon Soul Revival dug back up in Ho Chi Minh City in 2016, after a handful of musicians found a compilation called Saigon Rock & Soul: Vietnamese Classic Tracks 1968-1974 by Seattle label Sublime Frequencies, and realised nobody was playing that music live anymore. Nhạc kích động, the Western-influenced rock and soul strand of the period, had been banned outright after the war, while gentler nhạc vàng ballads survived. They started as a covers band and ended up writing most of their own catalogue instead. Ten years on, they carry it to WOMEX in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria this October. The band is Nguyễn Anh Minh on vocals, Indy Jeremy Vinh Laville on guitar and đàn nguyệt, Nguyễn Hương Bảo Hiếu on drums, Gabriel Kaouros on bass and percussion, and Đăng Nguyễn Khoa on keys, with traditional player Nguyễn Thị Hải Phượng guesting on đàn tranh and đàn bầu across their records. Their 2019 debut, Họa Âm Xưa, picked up airplay from Iggy Pop’s BBC6 show and France’s Radio FIP. Their second album, Mối Lương Duyên (2024), featured the single “Đám Cưới Nhà Em”, which went on to soundtrack a scene in HBO’s The Sympathizer. That December, the band recorded a live session for KEXP at l’Antipode in Rennes during TransMusicales. Their third album, Chốn Ta Về, releases 11 September via Saigon Supersound, folding in the T’rung bamboo xylophone and the sáo trúc flute alongside guest spots from multi-instrumentalist Đinh Nhật Minh and saxophonist Trần Mạnh Tuấn. From their WOMEX showcase, the band heads straight into a UK and Europe run: Musicport Festival in Whitby on 24 October, London’s Jazz Cafe the next night, then Bristol and Manchester, before continuing through mainland Europe to a Berlin date on 6 November. Below, the band talks about what it means to bring back music that was banned once already, and what they hope it means to a generation of young Vietnamese listeners discovering it for the first time. They also curate a playlist of the tracks that shaped their sound, exclusively for Rhythm Passport. For someone who’s never heard Nhạc Vàng, how would you describe what the band does, and what that sound felt like in the city it came from? Imagine being a teenager in Saigon, Vietnam in the late 1960s. Your grandparents are at a Cải Lương theater watching a traditional form of folk opera, your parents are singing along to a heartfelt nhạc vàng record in a typical Vietnamese bolero style, your auntie is going to a ballroom to dance the cha-cha-cha and on your way to the night market you pass by an American GI bar where a Vietnamese band is playing fuzzed out rock and twist songs for a young lively audience. All this while there is a war raging in the country with no end in sight. As a band we try to capture the essence of this period and imagine what it may have been like if the music of that time continued to develop without interruption until the present day. This music was effectively erased after 1975, when Western pop was banned and replaced. What drew the five of you to dig it back up rather than write something new, and how did you first find your way into these songs? Many classic nhạc vàng songs survived after 1975 and are popular to this day in Vietnam, but the more western influenced dance music, nhạc kích động, which were commonly in the styles of rock, surf, twist and soul were strictly banned and therefore were mostly unknown. When some of the members of SSR came across the compilation “Saigon Rock & Soul: Vietnamese Classic Tracks 1968-1974” we were blown away by the heavy raw sound and were amazed that these old songs were not being performed live to our knowledge, at least not the old versions. This inspired us to look more into such old recordings and start a tribute band to bring that energy back to the stage. You put rock musicians alongside players of the đàn nguyệt and đàn bầu, and let bolero sit next to psychedelia. What makes your version of this revival different from simply covering the originals? Though we started as a tribute band playing cover versions of these old 1960s/70s recordings and trying to really achieve that vintage sound, we eventually started making our own interpretations and ended up writing our own music entirely. In fact most of the songs on our albums are original compositions, many of which incorporate traditional Vietnamese instrumentation and fuse different styles in a very contemporary fashion. We always try to be true to our original inspiration and there are some old songs that are too good not to play, however our live shows and releases mainly consist of original material which we are happy to say has been received very positively. WOMEX is a room full of people who book, release and champion music from everywhere. Who or what are you hoping to connect with while you’re there? For us it’s an amazing opportunity to be able to perform at WOMEX and since Vietnam is not a country that is very present in the international music industry, we feel very privileged to be a part of such a globally recognised event. We do not have a specific agenda but we hope that we can make some good connections that will allow us to share our music and Vietnamese culture further across the world! You’ve built the band on raw, live shows: you’ve described the sound as descending out of the southern night sky. How does playing to a room of industry delegates, rather than a festival crowd, change the way you play? It’s hard to say because this will be our first time performing for a room of industry delegates haha. However, we have played several function gigs for embassies/consulates, hotels etc. and we always manage to connect with our audience and have them dancing by the end of the show. Your music resurrects a specific place and moment: the Saigon of the 1960s and 70s, dense and humid and electric. What’s it like to carry that sound to somewhere as far from it as a small Atlantic island, and does where you play change how it lands? Every place we play at has its own culture and vibe so it’s a pleasure for us to see how people react across the world. We are humans after all so we flow with and adapt to the energy at every show. That being said, we believe that wherever we play, it is our duty to create an atmosphere where people feel immersed in the music and energy we bring. Bringing back suppressed music is an act of memory as much as performance. What do you hope younger Vietnamese listeners, and audiences abroad who don’t know this history, take from it? We live in a very modern technological age where young people are increasingly valuing superficial entertainment and material wealth more than real culture. We hope to encourage the youth around the world to see the value in live performances and we especially wish to inspire our younger Vietnamese listeners to feel proud of their heritage, to appreciate and seek the roots of their culture. That is truly something worth valuing. Your new album Chốn Ta Về means “the place we return to.” What’s the homecoming in it, and where does the band go afterwards: more originals, more digging into the golden era, touring? Chốn Ta Về does not only refer to a literal home or country. The songs on the album tell different stories including ones of love, loss, resilience and acceptance. It’s not so much a matter of identity but a reference to finding our internal peace and our place in this world, no matter what the circumstances. If you could write a personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and discover your showcase, what would it say? ¡Ahul a toda la gente linda de las Islas Canarias! It’s not everyday you get to hear a Vietnamese band that fuses traditional ethnic sounds with heavy contemporary grooves and psychedilia. We will take you on a journey like no other. ¡Dale! Let’s get loose and show us how you party in Las Palmas!   Saigon Soul Revival carry the fuzzed-out rock and soul of wartime Saigon into WOMEX 2026 in Las Palmas on 21 October   PLAYLIST: SAIGON SOUL REVIVAL X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Saigon Soul Revival appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: “Kutsal Zeytin Halayı” traces one symbol across four thousand years: an olive branch carried in the beak of Noah’s dove, oil burning in lamps built for the Pharaohs, the same tree standing sacred on the Mount of Olives and sworn on in the Quran’s Fig Surah. BaBa Zula‘s Murat Ertel and Esma Ertel trade the lines between them, closing every turn of that history on the same vow: “I swear by that olive.” The song moves at a steady motorik pace, running the Istanbul band’s Anatolian psych roots into the dub and electronic experimentation they’ve pursued since 1996. Where the lyric’s mythology looks backward, its politics look straight at now: the band set the olive tree against what they call “corporate techno-fascism,” standing on nature’s side through every verse. It’s the first single from XXX, BaBa Zula’s new album, due on Glitterbeat on 25 September, at a tight thirty minutes and thirty seconds, the shortest and most focused record the band has made. Levent Akman, Ümit Adakale and Esma Ertel remain the same rhythm section that helped spark Turkey’s psychedelic revival three decades ago, joined here by guests İklim Tamkan on synth and organ and Eylül Güntekin on double bass. items.body: Review by martindavey87 — Recorded in 1969 and released in 1970, 'Concerto For Group and Orchestra' was the first live album by rock legends Deep Purple. It was the first major collaboration between a rock band and an orchestra, and it was the bands forth release in the span of three years. It's also the first album to feature vocalist Ian Gillan. It's actually quite an important release in the bands history.Unheard-of by today's work standards, but back then the band was incredibly ambitious and had an insane work ethic. With that said, however, this project is kind of a dud to my ears. The love child of keyboardist Jon Lord, the band's future depended on the success of this album, or the rock-oriented 'Deep Purple in Rock'. Thankfully, the 'In Rock' album prevailed and the band continued down their hard rock road to legendary status.As for 'Concerto', umm? it's not for me. I love Deep Purple, and admire their efforts to try something new, but I'm just not really keen to sit and listen to classical music like this. The first disc, featuring three Purple tracks is fine, but not anything I'd rush out to listen to. The band have incredible chemistry live and play their hearts out, but ultimately it's the hour-long love letter to classical music that is the most focal point of this album, and I'd much rather hear some hard and heavy rocking!Overall, there's one or two nice moments throughout the concerto itself, and it certainly works fine as background music, but I've given it multiple listens over a number of weeks, and I just don't have the patience anymore. This just isn't for me.

items.body: Review by greenpete — No sense in repeating everything already said about this rock masterwork, maybe the greatest debut ever. So I'll just provide a song rundown."Break on Through (To the Other Side)": the first single, and maybe the definitive Doors song. Beastly, guttural, and relentless, I've always thought of it as an aural interpretation of sexual intercourse. But that's just me."Soul Kitchen": sneering and funky, and a perfect follow-up to the opener. Something strange is being cooked up in this kitchen. Not sure what it is, but it's pulling me inside."The Crystal Ship": a gorgeous song. Drummer John Densmore has said it's about Morrison's breakup with a girlfriend, but there are many other interpretations."Twentieth Century Fox": this song ties in Morrison's and organist Ray Manzarek's film studies at UCLA. But I don't think Morrison is singing about Shirley Temple."Alabama Song (Whisky Bar)": written by Bertolt Brecht and Kurt Weill, from their satirical opera, Rise and Fall of the City of Mahagonny. It's the song that convinced Elektra founder Jac Holzman to sign the Doors, after seeing them perform it at the Whisky a Go Go in L.A. One of the strangest covers ever chosen for a rock LP, it nonetheless shows how eclectic the band was."Light My Fire": written by guitarist Robbie Krieger, the short version of the Doors' second single climbed to No. 1 in July 1967, and the band never looked back. The album version, with both a keyboard and guitar solo, is far more riveting. Jos� Feliciano had a No. 3 hit with a Latin-tinged acoustic rendition."Back Door Man": a lot of old blues songs were covered in the '60s, most not very well. One notable exception is Cream's version of Robert Johnson's "Cross Road Blues." Another is this Willie Dixon song, which the Doors made into their own. Morrison was still in the soul kitchen, only now he was sampling long-legged chicken."I Looked at You"/"End of the Night"/"Take it As It Comes": I lumped these three songs together because they're similar in tone and structure and seem to comprise three sections of one song, and they also provide a slow glide into the final song. Dark and sinister, the key song/line for me is "Some are born to sweet delight/Some are born to the endless night." The universe can be a hostile and indifferent place.Suddenly, we arrive at?"The End": I didn't know what to make of this 12-minute epic when I first heard it. It's less a song than a series of short poems set to psychedelic raga. Morrison sounds like he's intoning a dark sermon, taking the voyeuristic listener on a weird journey into goldmines, riding on snakes and blue buses. The section about the killer walking down the hall is chilling (Truman Capote's seminal non-fiction novel "In Cold Blood" was published just before the song was recorded).Unbelievably, "The End" was recorded in only two takes. According to Holzman, the second half of Take 2 was so intense that, as the closing notes faded, producer Paul Rothchild turned to him in the booth, and with a stunned look said "Jac, this is why we do what we do."This is one of my Top 10 Desert Isle Albums, and "Light My Fire" my numero uno song, which always takes me back to 1967. So a very, very easy five stars.

items.body: Review by kenfromlaisve — Cathedral ? Stained Glass Stories: A Masterclass MisunderstoodStained Glass Stories stands as one of the great lost artifacts of 1970s American independent music. Self-released in 1978 via Delta Records - a fiercely DIY operation situated above the Palace Theater in Times Square - this singular statement by New York's Cathedral remains one of my absolute favourite albums. It is a record that demands attention not just for what it is, but for what it firmly is not. There is a persistent, lazy critical shorthand that attempts to dismiss Cathedral as merely derivative of the British symphonic prog giants. As a longtime listener of both Genesis and Yes, I find these claims entirely baseless. If the band were simply tracing the outlines of their predecessors, the similarities would be glaringly obvious - yet they aren't there. How any reviewer can draw a line between this record and Genesis's Nursery Cryme is baffling; the two albums share zero overlap in texture, architecture, or intent. Cathedral wasn't mimicking the old guard; they were constructing their own highly complex, insular soundscapes from the ground up.The true anchor of this album - and a reason it is essential listening for any student of the instrument - is the sublime bass playing of Fred Callan. Often utilizing Moog bass pedals to widen the low-end spectrum, Callan's work weaves through the intricate arrangements with a commanding, lyrical presence. Nowhere is this more apparent than on my favourite track, 'Gong'. It is an absolute masterclass in instrumental tension, anchoring the band's most ambitious rhythmic ideas. Yet, to single out one track almost feels unfair to the cohesive brilliance of the pressing. The quality simply never subsides. From the sweeping, twelve-minute-plus opener 'Introspect' to the labyrinthine structural shifts of 'Days & Changes' and the closing epic 'The Search', the momentum never wavers. The band - rounded out by Tom Doncourt's expansive keyboard textures and Mercury Caronia IV's exhaustive percussion arsenal - managed to capture lightning in a bottle, tracking the material largely live to a sixteen-track Ampex machine. The only lingering downer surrounding Stained Glass Stories is its isolation in the archives. It is a profound pity that we do not have a more exhaustive canon of work from such a remarkable group. While the band eventually regrouped decades later to release a belated sophomore effort, 2007's The Bridge, one can only imagine the discography that might have materialized had they been afforded the runway they deserved during their initial run.

items.body: Review by alainPP — The album's centerpiece is undoubtedly the 'Medley Dark Ages Suite: Power and Bread / En de Nux / Time For Monsters / Ouroboros / Renaissance.' It delivers a new-millennium neo-sound?riff-heavy, energetic, and eager to tackle progressive metal head-on. It unfolds across four movements, starting with a shimmering intro featuring piano, Moog, and all the stylistic trimmings. The shift from snarling vocals against a symphonic backdrop to roaring guitars offers a refreshing change of pace. With a dash of flute, the influences are diverse?echoes of Jethro Tull in the distance and Schulze for the electronic elements. It is intense, complex, and even chaotic at times?featuring distant sirens and Floyd-esque vocoders?yet it works. The interwoven vocals of Stefano and Beatrice create the perfect synergy and depth to narrate the human dilemma regarding AI?a tale as old as time. A medieval touch emerges midway through, with delicate piano notes cascading alongside an austere violin and cinematic sheep sounds. The third quarter offers instrumental symphonic depth, leading into an electro-neo renaissance?a rock-opera finale with spellbinding vocals. It combines the velvety synth tones of yesteryear with a cutting-edge neo-prog sound, capped off by a space-diving outro that hits hard.The live set features four tracks from the latest album and one from the debut. 'Hamlet's Mill Ouverture' kicks things off with a barrage of synths, haughty vocals, and heavy guitars?delivering an epic, relentless, and hard-hitting progressive metal sound. 'Key to the Temple' begins with a distinctive symphonic style?layered arrangements and sharp riffs backing Stefano's edgy vocals?before shifting to a delicate interplay with Beatrice during the infectious chorus. This live performance sees them transition from neo-prog to neo-prog-metal?a spirited and emotional display. The sound is reminiscent of Clive Nolan's work. "C'e Casa a 30 Miglia" stands out for the delicate interplay of melancholic guitar over piano?a sugary-sweet ballad with broad appeal, driven by evocative Italian vocals. "Paths of the Sky"?an excerpt from the original 17-minute "Possessed by Time"?blends B�atrice's spellbinding vocals with Simone's tribal pads; a folk-medieval flute and Hammond organ then join in on this meltingly lovely, nursery-rhyme-like tune. Finally, "Dance of the Stars" features a swirling violin melody that feels truly starry. It has a vintage vibe that reinforces their live prowess?ensuring fans aren't just sitting in armchairs before heading back to the retirement home for the night.An album that truly warrants a comeback and offers a refreshing change of pace from standard RPI.

items.body: Review by Matti — I found the music of SUPERTRAMP as a teenager in 1987, and I quite soon I also purchased (second-hand) two solo albums of the band's ex-member, vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Roger Hodgson, who was IMHO definitely the band's better song-writer. Whereas In the Eye of the Storm (1984) had pretty good stuff in it, Hai Hai (1987) was a disastrous let-down as a horribly produced eighties pop album.'Land Ho' was a new version of the song which was recorded in December 1973 by Supertramp's newly born classic line-up and released as a single the following spring when they had started working on their breakthrough album Crime of the Century (1974). Therefor the song is jointly credited to Roger Hodgson & Rick Davies, like all Supertramp songs up to 1982's Famous Last Words, despite being solely Hodgson's composition. As an upbeat, lighthearted song it's quite OK, perhaps remotely reminiscent of -- but not half as good as -- 'Dreamer' from Crime of the Century. Back then I didn't know its 70's origins. I guess I just hastily listened to the album a couple of times, horrified by the bad production (that ruins this song, too), before returning it to circulation.The harder rocking 'My Magazine' must have sounded awful to my ears on every level right from the start, as it does right now. Roger even sings it with a ballsy rock attitude that doesn't suit him at all. The song is amazingly dull as a repetitive composition. There were guys from TOTO (Paich, Porcaro) and other undoubtedly fine musicians playing on the album, but it was the late 80's, one of the worst periods of pop music when it comes to the production style. Noisy drums and all.I never waste my time returning to entire albums I have strongly disliked on the first listen, nor reviewing albums that I'd see worth of one star only. So excuse me this 7" review.

items.body: Review by progtime1234567 — It was only recently when I discovered that I really like this band. Even though I've been a fan ofprogressive rock/metal since around 2018, I only ever listened to Pawn Hearts by this band. WhilePawn Hearts is obviously a great album, I think I'm a bigger fan of this album. Van der Graaf Generator is one of those darker-ish sounding prog bands, sort of in the same vein asKing Crimson. For example, the first song "Killer", which is one of the more accessible songs bythis band, deals with themes of loneliness and death. The lyrics describe a shark that kills therest of the fish around it. I take this as a metaphor for someone who pushes everyone away fromthem, despite wanting to have relationships with the people around them. The song's introspectivelyrics are typical for progressive rock, but it is still a far cry from bands like Yes, whose themesusually revolve around literature, but can occasionally deal with darker themes (see the Yes Album). I personally think Van der Graaf Generator is one of the better progressive rock bands from the1970s. Although they never reached the same levels of commercial success like their peers Yes orGenesis, they were very influential on progressive rock and progressive metal. Similarly to KingCrimson, Van der Graaf Generator is your favorite band's favorite band. This album, along with PawnHearts and Godbluff make a solid trilogy of albums.

items.body: Review by greenpete — I've never considered this one-of-a-kind record even close to what we might classify as "prog." But it's listed here on Progressive Archives (with gratitude) so here goes:Scholars of European history might recognize Balaklava (also spelled with a 'c', "Balaclava") as the name of the place where a famous British cavalry charge occurred in 1854 during the Crimean War. The poet�Alfred, Lord Tennyson immortalized it in his poem about valor,�The Charge of the Light Brigade. The truth is that this charge was an unnecessary military action, a suicidal maneuver that dissolved 40 percent of an entire brigade. Valor in suicide. Irony, like this, was a Tom Rapp specialty.The year 1968 had a similarly senseless military action going on, this one in Southeast Asia. More irony: Rapp dedicated his record to WWII soldier Eddie Slovik, the only U.S. soldier executed for desertion since the American Civil War."Some people thought (my) songs were hopeless. I was being realistic about the pain that's out there. If you say life is wonderful, people know it isn't true, but if you talk about the pain, someone will listen." (Tom Rapp, from "Crawdaddy," December 2008)"Tears are often jewel-like."The first thing that makes�Balaklava�different from other records is its unusual sleeve art. Album reproductions of paintings later became popular, but�Balaklava�is one of the first examples, and the painting chosen partially relates to the music inside. It's a reproduction of Pieter Brueghel the Elder's 16th-century, apocalyptic oil panel "The Triumph of Death," with typewriter characters of the band name and album title stamped across the top, as if this record is a dispatch being wired from the abyss below.The back cover features surreal illustrations by French avant-garde writer and filmmaker Jean Cocteau. Also, a quote from American philosopher and poet�George Santayana: "Only the dead have seen the end of war." And yet more irony: a photograph of a freckle-faced girl wearing a shy smile, with a daisy protruding from her plaid dress, and a button reading "Pearls Before Swine." (The photo was snapped at a peace rally by photographer Mel Zimmer. The girl's button actually said "Flower Power." Zimmer identifies his photo as "Molly Stewart.")So, the listener has an idea where this record is headed even before the needle strikes the wax. The packaging is deliberate and unapologetic. As Dante wrote in "The Inferno:"�All hope abandon, ye who enter here.Another striking thing about�Balaklava: the music is introduced by a ghost. The first "song" is titled "Trumpeter Landfrey," and is the actual voice and bugle call of a survivor of the Light Brigade charge, a man named Martin Leonard Landfried. With brimming pride,�Landfried announces, "I am now going to sound the bugle that was sounded at Waterloo, and sound the charge that was sounded at Balaklava on that very same bugle, the 25th�of October, 1854." Landfried's scratchy voice comes from a cylinder recording from 1890 that was reissued on a vinyl record that�Rapp owned.Landfried's bugle notes smoothly segue into the strummed guitar notes of "Translucent Carriages." Wikipedia calls this one of Rapp's "most enduring songs," a shivering tune whose title again harkens to yesteryear, and whose languid music includes ghostly background whisperings. One of them is the Herodotus quote "In peace, sons bury their fathers / In war, fathers bury their sons." Another is the Rapp quote "Jesus raised the dead / But who will raise the living?"The recurring chorus goes "Every time I see you, passing by, I have to wonder, why?" The identity of the "you" can be interpreted differently. Are they ancient carriages, perhaps Roman? Hearses? Maybe a woman? Is Rapp referring to Jesus? Or the pointlessness of war?"Images of April" burrows deeper into the murky surreal. It features vocal echoes, flute, bird songs, and even frog croaks to paint a world of desolation, where�springtime exists in�fleeting images that only memory can summon. If you're open to something strange, hypnotic, and completely different:As unconventional as is "Images of April," the next song, "There Was a Man," is totally conventional - the guitar/vocal music, that is. The words, maybe less so. They relate a story about a stranger who one day arrives in a village. The stranger has a scar on his head, "where there used to be a crown." He amazes the people by doing wonderful, magical things. Then the stranger leaves, sadly, suddenly. He has heard "the news from the war.""I Saw the World" is maybe the most passionate song on�Balaklava. Rapp pleads, with palpable emotion in his voice,�that he's seen the world "spinning like a toy," and "hate seems so small compared to it all." A melodious cello and piano passage helps boost this song to another plane.Rapp was an admirer of songwriter Leonard Cohen, and the Pearls honor him with a rendition of Cohen's "Suzanne." They supposedly recorded this song in one take, while sitting on the studio floor, in the dark, with candles burning. (Yes, very Sixties.) The hushed ambience they created must have succeeded, since this is one of the most respectfully rendered versions of this acclaimed song. Other titles include "Guardian Angels" and "Lepers and Roses," both of which further the odd, time-frozen quality of�Balaklava. At the end of the record, there's another vintage 1890 recording, this one of Florence Nightengale, who oversaw the nurses during the Crimean War. She prays that her Balaklava "comrades" will all return "safe to shore." The record trails off with Trumpeter Landfried's opening again.�It's a reminder that everything is a circle, that everything "comes back again,"�both love and hate.While not a perfect record - it loses steam at the very end - and certainly not for every ear,�Balaklava's�best moments�overflow with�a perceptiveness, mystery, and beauty not usually occurring in rock music. Today, we hear the word "alternative," which means "different" or "unconventional," applied to�a certain style of music (for the sake of convenience, branding, and marketing).� But Pearls Before Swine's�Balaklava�defines the word alternative.� There's�not another record like it.Even more, the record is a unique and fervent indictment of the idea that warfare is some kind of glorious endeavor. It is music with meaning.�But unlike most anti-war artists of the Sixties - idealistic and well-meaning, but who relied on anthems or derivative platitudes about peace and love - Tom mRapp used irony, surrealism, and religious and historical allusions to present his worldview. He drew from a war in 1854 to indict a war of 1968, which still resonates today.(4 stars instead of 5 only because it's not "prog" and spirit this intense could never sustain a full LP)

items.body: Every spectacle contains a private bargain with disaster. Fireworks make that bargain visible: powder and metal are prepared for beauty, ignited at close range, and trusted to travel in the promised direction. When the trajectory fails, celebration becomes panic before the eye can separate pleasure from fear. A relationship ruled by manipulation follows a similar course. Possession borrows the language of protection, dependency passes for devotion, and the danger becomes obvious only after the fuse has already burned its way down. Australian witch house and dream pop duo dusk2dawn place that collision at the center of It Kills Me Every Time. The downtempo lament is the second single from their debut album, Make A Wish, due September 11, 2026, through DERO Arcade. It follows Psalm 23, the record’s first official single, released in July. The recording opens in a distant hum that could be a roadway heard through concrete, then sinks into a deeper metallic drone. Synthesizers spread outward in broad, gauzy layers, carrying something of Blade Runner’s nocturnal grandeur through the haze of shoegaze and dreampop. A slow, shuffling drumbeat gives the track its narcotized gait. Jack Mannix sings with a dull, depleted sorrow, his voice seemingly drawn from a heart where hope has been reduced to residue. Finn Parker keeps widening the arrangement behind him, laying sheet after sheet of synth across the rhythm until the music reaches the desolate scale of The Cure’s slowest pieces on Disintegration and Wish. Written around manipulation, betrayal, boredom, possession, and dependency, It Kills Me Every Time dwells inside an attachment where harm has repeated so often that it begins to feel like the governing law. The measured tempo gives every phrase room to sink in, while the massed keyboards turn sorrow into something physical, pressing against the vocal from all sides. The accompanying video extends that condition into a catalogue of amateur fireworks disasters. Grainy found footage shows driveways, parking lots, wet plazas, and crowded public displays briefly transformed by fountains and rockets that veer sideways, topple, or burst at ground level. People scatter as white flashes burn out the camera sensor; cars and houses disappear behind red smoke; one doomed attempt gives way to another. Edited by Parker from clips sourced by Mannix, the film finds a grimly apt image for the song’s damaged intimacy: people remain close to something designed to explode because they still want the promised beauty. “We often work with found footage for our videos, previously we have used footage of an exotic dancer in a masonic lodge, or a montage of controlled building demolitions. I like the way that these visuals provide an emotional metaphor for the music and create a somewhat hypnotic and disturbing viewing experience, with the aesthetics of lost media and youtube rabbit holes. For this video the firework accident footage seemed fitting as it was this document of people creating these dangerous and beautiful displays of explosives, and an attempt at one thing that goes wrong and creates another. The lengths and risks people will endure for a spectacle” Watch the video for It Kills Me Every Time below: dusk2dawn brings Finn Parker of Eternal Dust together with Jack Mannix of Circle Pit. The two first met as teenagers within Sydney’s post-punk scene and briefly played in a band alongside future members of Low Life and Exek. Parker began dusk2dawn as a solo outlet for the witch house- and gabber-informed instrumentals he was making while active in Eternal Dust, inviting Mannix to join as vocalist and lyricist in late 2022. Early demos followed during a brief period when they shared an apartment in Kings Cross and were released through Mannix’s DERO Arcade. A handful of sold-out appearances in Sydney and Melbourne accompanied the pair’s work on what would become Make A Wish. Across the album, dusk2dawn move from the punk and industrial pressure of opening track Angel Face into dream pop and witch house ballads such as soul2keep, Heaven Is Only In Hell, and Gateway. Psalm 23, the title track, and Behind The Mask draw the record toward darker gothic forms. Its subjects remain equally severe, moving among suffering, grief, sublimation, transcendence, decay, mutation, and possession. Of his approach to the lyrics, Mannix says: “I try to make my lyrics for this project as obtuse and simple as possible, to create a screen that the listener can easily project their own experiences and interpretations onto. I want to cast a spell that is at once loaded and universal – the real meaning buried in the simplest possible terms.” Make A Wish was recorded and mixed by Finn Parker and Eduardo Bianchino, then mastered by Wayne Sunderland at Suture Mastering. The album arrives September 11 through DERO Arcade. Listen to It Kills Me Every Time below and pre-order the album here. items.body: New York producer BrokinPaper releases his album “Function Over Form” on 9 September 2026. The seven-track record includes the previously released singles “Damage”, “Antidote Remix” (featuring Jenasi) and “Malice”, alongside four unreleased tracks. BrokinPaper is the solo project of Queens-born producer Harrison Lee, who describes the album’s sound as industrial techno mixed with UK garage, bass and electro. Lee has spoken of the album as a deliberate shift toward tracks built for DJ sets rather than home listening. He told UKF: “This one feels more intentional on hitting the bass market and shifting gears a bit. I’ve had more DJ opportunities recently, and instead of maybe curating a vibe that you can listen to at home, for this project I’m being intentional about creating something that is more exciting to hear live.” A pitch email for the album describes it as BrokinPaper’s debut album; but Bandcamp also lists an earlier full-length, “Creation Theory” (2023). BrokinPaper has drawn attention outside music in 2026: he DJed the “GucciCore” afterparty tied to Gucci’s Cruise 2027 show in Times Square and the Gucci Berlin Gallery Weekend afterparty, and Beatport named him one of its emerging artists to watch in July 2026. He recorded a 60-minute guest mix for HÖR Berlin and was named Billboard’s Dance Artist of the Month for September 2026. About BrokinPaper BrokinPaper is the solo project of Harrison Lee, born and raised in Queens, New York. He began producing as a teenager in 2009, first making hip-hop beats on FL Studio before moving toward darker, more minimal electronic production influenced by Gesaffelstein, RL Grime, Hudson Mohawke, TNGHT and Lunice. The 2019 EP “The Maslow EP”, which included “Sapiosexuality”, marked the point where the BrokinPaper sound took its current form. The project’s name comes from Broken Paper Wings, a metal band Lee tried to start as a teenager. BrokinPaper’s music has been placed in a ZARA holiday hair campaign and the Peacock series “M.I.A.”, both using the track “66023C”, and has drawn support from Timbaland and REZZ, including a DJ mix for REZZ’s label HypnoVizion. “Function Over Form”, arriving 9 September 2026, follows the 2023 album “Creation Theory” and leads a planned companion project, “Form Over Function”, described by Lee as a lighter, more melodic counterpart.

items.body: German synth duo Felsmann + Tiley released Echonomist’s remix of “God Is Lonelier” on 3 September 2026. The original, featuring Laius, comes from the duo’s Mute album “Protomensch”, released on 13 February 2026. Dominik Felsmann and Patrick Tiley also announced two live dates: London’s Purcell Room on 22 November and Berlin’s Kantine am Berghain on 25 November. Echonomist worked on the remix while touring the US and Mexico, finishing most of it in a friend’s studio in Los Angeles. He “worked on this remix while touring across the US and Mexico, with most of it coming together in a friend’s studio in LA. It feels like the soundtrack to all those long drives, flights and quiet hours between shows. Spending so much time on the road, away from home, made the whole process feel even more emotional, and I think that naturally found its way into the remix.” “God Is Lonelier” is the fourth entry in a remix series drawn from “Protomensch”: Sofi Paez reworked “Reset”, Lambert reworked “Open Fields”, Lysten remixed “Warum” and Sensu took on “Always You”. Felsmann + Tiley say more reinterpretations are coming from Meredi, Jamie Irrepressible and Silver Panda, among others. Live dates 22 Nov 2026 – London, UK – Purcell Room, Southbank Centre 25 Nov 2026 – Berlin, DE – Kantine am Berghain About Felsmann + Tiley Dominik Felsmann and Patrick Tiley met in 2003 on the German music production forum MyOwnMusic.de and discovered they shared a hometown, Stuttgart, along with an interest in “the depth and melancholy of trance pads and breakdowns that always had a certain darkness to them.” As the alias Kamui they released the 12″ “Ghosts”, followed by releases under five further aliases on different labels. Their reinterpretation of The Irrepressibles’ “The Most Beautiful Boy” became the lead track for the second season of the Netflix series “Young Royals”, and their version of M83’s “Solitude” appeared on the British crime series “Top Boy”; both tracks, later released on Mute and Deutsche Grammophon, have reached a combined 200 million streams. Felsmann + Tiley signed to Mute and released the track “Warum” in June 2025, followed by the video for “Always You” (featuring Woodes) from “Protomensch” in February 2026. “Protomensch” (Mute/Embassy One) followed on 13 February 2026, featuring guest vocalists Pet Deaths, The Kite String Tangle, Woodes and Laius across its twelve tracks. Since then the duo has released a run of guest reinterpretations of album tracks, of which the Echonomist remix of “God Is Lonelier” is the latest, alongside their two newly announced November shows in London and Berlin.

items.body: Thirteen of the fourteen songs are already out; the running order is the news. Mycelium Sky, the one-man dark psychedelic industrial rock project of US musician Jacoboon (Jacob Reed), release the debut album “Hello World” on Saturday 5 September 2026 through the project’s own label Mindstorm Unlimited LLC. The album is digital only, runs 69 minutes and 17 seconds, and adds one previously unreleased track, the closer “Questions Remain”, to the thirteen singles issued between 31 January and 14 August 2026. The most recent of those, “Here We Fxn Go”, is on Spotify now. The project makes no secret of how the record was built. Its press page states: “Lyrics come first, written by hand. Music is generated with Suno; videos are grown […] with Neural Frames; structure, selection, and final cut stay human.” The credits list Jacoboon for lyrics, concept, direction and edit, Suno for the music, Mixea for mastering and DistroKid for distribution; the videos come from that same AI video platform, except “Asking Questions” (made with Sora) and “Welcome to Earth M.F.” (Kling). One lyric is the exception: the words to “Roots on the Glass” were written by the AI, and the record credits it as such. “My Country” builds on two public-domain texts, Samuel Francis Smith’s 1831 “America” and A. G. Duncan’s 1843 abolitionist rewrite from “Anti-Slavery Melodies”. Mycelium Sky mix mechanical atmospheres, ritual-style lyrics and rock songwriting, and name Tool, A Perfect Circle, Nine Inch Nails, Puscifer and darkwave as their reference points. Tracklist and mirror structure of ‘Hello World’ The fourteen tracks are sequenced as seven pairs that fold around a break between tracks 7 and 8, with each song in the second half answering its counterpart in the first: 1 with 14, 2 with 13, and so on. Jacoboon says the structure was found rather than designed: the album was thirteen tracks deep when one change to the running order locked the fold, moving “Lie to Me” from track 2 to track 5 and sending “Questions Remain”, until then track 8, to the end to answer the opener. The pivot pairs “Safety in Solitude” and “No Escape”, two songs the project describes as performing the same act with opposite outcomes. The running order, with single release dates: 1. “Asking Questions” (31 January), 2. “First Impression” (31 January), 3. “Roots on the Glass” (31 January), 4. “Option 2” (27 February), 5. “Lie to Me” (31 January), 6. “Fall in Line” (20 March), 7. “Safety in Solitude” (10 April), 8. “No Escape” (1 May), 9. “My Country” (25 May), 10. “Welcome to Earth M.F.” (12 June), 11. “The Misunderstood” (3 July), 12. “Strange but True” (24 July), 13. “Here We Fxn Go” (14 August), 14. “Questions Remain” (5 September). “Lie to Me”, “Fall in Line”, “Welcome to Earth M.F.” and “Here We Fxn Go” carry explicit tags. Pre-saves run through DistroKid’s HyperFollow page, and the singles are on Spotify, Apple Music, Deezer and iHeartRadio, among other services. About Mycelium Sky Mycelium Sky is the solo project of Jacoboon, who writes the lyrics and concepts, directs the AI tools and makes the final cut, and releases the results on his own Mindstorm Unlimited LLC. The project’s first chapter was the music video for “Asking Questions” in December 2025, followed by the first four singles on 31 January 2026 and a further nine through 14 August. A glowing red question mark recurs across every cover and video. Alongside the songs, the project runs the Tone Garden, a generative ambient instrument tuned in just intonation, on its website. The project’s press contact is handled by AI assistants that identify themselves as such; Jacoboon answers in his own name on request. “Hello World” on 5 September 2026 is Mycelium Sky’s first album and the first time the fourteen tracks appear in their mirrored sequence.

items.body: Fifty years to the day after Throbbing Gristle played the ICA as part of their “Prostitution” exhibition, the London gallery hosts TG50, a day of films, talks, music and merchandise on Sunday 18 October 2026. Throbbing Gristle – Cosey Fanni Tutti, Chris Carter, Genesis Breyer P-Orridge (1950-2020) and Peter “Sleazy” Christopherson (1955-2010) – date their start to 3 September 1976, and the announcement lands on that anniversary. The same day, Mute opens registration for “TG24+”, a limited-edition USB box set with 36 live performances newly mastered and restored by Chris Carter, due on 4 December 2026. The event is free to attend and runs as a drop-in through the day, with separate paid tickets for the limited-capacity cinema screenings and talks. The screening programme has not been announced yet. One item is already on sale: Chris Carter and Cosey Fanni Tutti in conversation with Luke Turner, editor of The Quietus, at 6pm in Cinema 2. The ICA says the two will “reflect on the early days of Throbbing Gristle, their experience of London at the time, and the ways in which they forged new forms of music and art amid the city’s cultural underground”. The day also launches a new range of TG merchandise, with some items sold only at the event. The ICA presents TG50 in partnership with Mute. TG50 at the ICA on 18 October 2026 The date is not random. “Prostitution”, the October 1976 exhibition by the performance group COUM Transmissions at the ICA, doubled as the public debut of Throbbing Gristle, and the band’s performance there took place on 18 October 1976. The show drew the headlines “MP’s fury at porn palace” (Daily Mirror) and “Bust-up at Gallery of Porn” (Daily Express), and Conservative MP Nicholas Fairbairn called the group “wreckers of civilisation” in Parliament. That phrase later became the title of Simon Ford’s 1999 book on COUM and TG. The ICA describes TG50 as a day that brings fans together “to share memories, stories and reflections on the band and what their work has meant to them”. The band returned to the same building in June 2007 for a three-day recording session, sold afterwards as the 12-CD “The Desertshore Installation”. “TG24+” continues a series that began in 1980, when Industrial Records issued “TG24” as a box of 24 cassettes covering the band’s first 24 concerts. Mute reissued it as a CD box in December 2002, with 26 performances, and followed it with “TG+”, which added ten more. The new USB edition carries 36 shows, the combined total of those two sets, in Chris Carter’s new masters. Pricing and the exact contents have not been published; Mute is taking registrations of interest ahead of the 4 December release. About Throbbing Gristle Throbbing Gristle grew out of COUM Transmissions, the performance group Genesis P-Orridge and Cosey Fanni Tutti ran in Kingston upon Hull before moving to Hackney, London in 1973. There they met Chris Carter, then a television sound recordist, and Peter Christopherson, then a member of the design collective Hipgnosis, and built a studio they named “The Death Factory”. The four went public as Throbbing Gristle at the ICA in October 1976 and set up their own label, Industrial Records, which gave the genre its name. “The Second Annual Report” (November 1977, first pressed in 786 copies) was followed by the single “United / Zyklon B Zombie”, “D.o.A: The Third and Final Report of Throbbing Gristle” (1978), “20 Jazz Funk Greats” (1979) and “Heathen Earth” (1980). In 1980 they also scored Neil Ruttenberg’s horror film “Mask of Sarnath”, a soundtrack that resurfaced last year on the “Mask of Sarnath” DVD. After a final show in San Francisco on 29 May 1981, the band mailed out postcards on 23 June 1981 declaring their mission terminated. The members split into Psychic TV (P-Orridge and Christopherson), Chris & Cosey and later Coil (Christopherson with John Balance). The 2002 “TG24” reissue on Mute preceded a reunion in 2004, which produced “TG Now”, a first comeback show at the London Astoria on 16 May 2004 and a set at All Tomorrow’s Parties in Camber Sands on 3 December 2004. “Part Two: The Endless Not” followed on 2 April 2007, recorded in Berlin, with shows at the Donaufestival in Krems, Tate Modern and the ICA installation the same year. A US tour in April 2009, including Coachella, coincided with “The Third Mind Movements”. P-Orridge left in October 2010, Christopherson died in November 2010, and Carter and Tutti finished the group’s work as X-TG with “Desertshore / The Final Report” (2012). P-Orridge died in March 2020. Mute has kept the catalogue in circulation since: the reissue series was “relaunched with ‘TGCD1’ and ‘The Third Mind Movements'” in July 2024, the previously unreleased track “Scabs & Saws” surfaced in October 2024, a “Hamburger Lady” live video arrived in April 2025 and “Live at the Volksbühne Berlin, New Year’s Eve 2005” came out in May 2025. Carter and Tutti continue to record as Carter Tutti and Carter Tutti Void, and Tutti was named the Innovator Award recipient at the AIM Independent Music Awards 2025. TG50 on 18 October 2026 returns the two surviving members to the room where the band first played, and “TG24+” on 4 December puts the live archive that started with the 1980 cassette box onto a single USB drive.

items.body: Two Twice a Man artbooks now land on the same day. The Swedish synthpop act release their new album “Reveries Before Silence” on 20 November 2026 through Dependent Records, as a 36-page hardcover 2CD artbook with lyrics and liner notes, limited to 500 copies. The first single, “Desert Snow”, is out now with a visualiser, with music and visuals by the band. Pre-orders run through the label store. Reveries Before Silence by Twice a Man The album runs to seven tracks: “Instruments of Joy”, “During Cloudtime”, “Constant Dreaming”, “Beating Still”, “Desert Snow”, “Lifeform” and “Rabbit Walk”. The artbook edition adds four bonus tracks, “Incredible Journeys”, “There Are Flowers to Grow”, “In A Coloured Cloud” and “A Foggy Slumber”. Twice a Man recorded and mixed the album at their own Xenophone Studio in Jörlanda, and Hans Olsson mastered it at Svenska Grammofonstudion in Gothenburg. The band also handled the artwork and layout. The current line-up is Dan Söderqvist on electronics, guitars and vocals, Karl Gasleben on electronics and Jocke Söderqvist on electronics. Dependent describes the record as “an open invitation to join a collective dance fuelled by electronic beats and melodies”. Gasleben, speaking for the band, called the single “one of our musical footprints in a time marked by uncertainty, division, and change”. He added: “This song reflects on the world we live in today while reminding us that hope and positive thinking can still be a path toward unity. As modern societies continue to challenge our sense of human connection, we need to find what brings us together rather than what drives us apart. […] ‘Desert Snow’ is our contribution to that conversation – a song that carries both reflection and faith in a better future.” ‘The Marine Trilogy’ moves to 20 November The companion release Side-Line covered in August, the 48-page 2CD artbook “The Marine Trilogy”, was announced for 23 October 2026. It now arrives on 20 November 2026, the same day as “Reveries Before Silence”. That set gathers the marine-themed material from the 1984 cassette “Waterland” and the 12″ singles “Across The Ocean” (1984) and “Aqua Marine Drum” (1986), remastered for their first appearance on CD, and is also limited to 500 copies. About Twice a Man Twice a Man come from Gothenburg, where Dan Söderqvist and Karl Gasleben met in the early 1970s in the groups Älgarnas Trädgård and Anna Själv Tredje. From 1978 the two worked as Cosmic Overdose, whose 1981 tape “Final Koko” was reissued in 2024, and took the Twice a Man name in 1981. The debut album “Music For Girls” followed in 1982, with “From a Northern Shore” (1984), “Slow Swirl” (1985) and “Works On Yellow” (1986) in the years after; from 1984 the group added samplers and field recordings to their synthesizer set-up. Alongside records, Twice a Man wrote music for seven full-evening productions at the Royal Dramatic Theatre in Stockholm, for a 1984 whale exhibition at the Cultural House of Stockholm, and for film, dance, exhibitions and the 1998 PlayStation game “Kula World”. Their catalogue in the following decades includes “Driftwood” (1988), “Agricultural Beauty” (2002), “Clouds” (2008), “Icicles” (2010), “Presence” (2015), the ambient forest album “Cocoon” (2019) and “On the Other Side of the Mirror” (2020). Jocke Söderqvist, a long-time collaborator, rejoined in 2013 and is credited on the recent albums. With Dependent Records the band compiled the 3CD artbook “Songs of Future Memories (1982-2022)”, announced in November 2022 with a video for “Decay”, and released the video “Dahlia” in February 2023. The single “Birds Eye View” opened the campaign for “The Coloured Breeze Is a New Dimension”, released on 13 June 2025 on vinyl and as a CD book. Earlier this year the German act Coloured Tears devoted two tribute albums to the band’s 1982-1988 songs. “Reveries Before Silence” is the second Twice a Man studio album on Dependent in under eighteen months, and the 20 November date pairs it with the mid-1980s recordings of “The Marine Trilogy”.

items.body: Three co-writers share the credits on the new PIG EP. “Dirt Box” is released on 4 September 2026 via Metropolis Records, on CD and digital, and collects four new songs by Raymond Watts plus a remix of each. The songs were written with Marc Heal of Cubanate and C-Tec, former KMFDM guitarist Günter Schulz and Watts’ regular writing partner Jim Davies, formerly of The Prodigy and Pitchshifter. The EP follows the album “Hurt People Hurt”, out since May, and lands a week after PIG opened a 44-date North American tour. Dirt Box by PIG Four new PIG songs and four remixes on ‘Dirt Box’ The opener, “An American Ideal Of Beauty”, came out as a single on 31 July with a video directed by E Gabriel Edvy; Side-Line covered it at the time (PIG release ‘An American Ideal Of Beauty’ single from ‘Dirt Box’ EP). Watts described the four-way studio line-up behind it as “my old partners in swine Marc and Günter” joining Davies and himself, with the single “the first result of our work as a quartet”. The same sessions produced “Your Reptilian Overlord Presents”, “Infidel” and “Butterfly”, which complete the first half of the record. The second half hands each song to a different remixer. Cyanotic, who are supporting PIG on the current tour, rework “Your Reptilian Overlord Presents”; Chris Hall of Stabbing Westward remixes “An American Ideal Of Beauty”; Combichrist take on “Butterfly”; and Rabbit Junk close the EP with “Infidel”. The full running order is: An American Ideal Of Beauty Your Reptilian Overlord Presents Infidel Butterfly Your Reptilian Overlord Presents (Cyanotic Remix) An American Ideal Of Beauty (Stabbing Westward Remix) Butterfly (Combichrist Remix) Infidel (Rabbit Junk Remix) The CD edition, sold through the Metropolis Records store, adds a ninth track, “Atrocity Obsession”, listed as a spoken-word bonus. The digital release on Bandcamp carries the eight tracks above. The EP arrives mid-tour. The Hurt People Tour started on 27 August in Lawrence, Kansas and runs to 18 October in Detroit, taking in Cold Waves XIV shows in Los Angeles on 11 September, Austin on 18 September and Chicago on 25 September. That last date is also when the “Merciless” remix vinyl arrives through Armalyte Industries, with reworks by Clock DVA, Pitchshifter, StabWalt and Schulz. Four UK shows follow in December. About PIG PIG is the project of Raymond Watts, born in London on 1 September 1961. In the mid-1980s he worked as a sound engineer for Einstürzende Neubauten and, in Hamburg, was a founding member of KMFDM, later returning to write and sing on the 1995 album “Nihil”. He played in Foetus and worked with Psychic TV, and released the first PIG album, “A Poke in the Eye… with a Sharp Stick”, in 1988. “Praise the Lard” (1991), “The Swining” (1993), “Sinsation” (1995), “Wrecked” (1996) and “Genuine American Monster” (1999) followed, several of them first issued in Japan, where Watts also sang with Schaft and Schwein. PIG opened for Nine Inch Nails in Europe in 1994, and “Sinsation” reached the United States through Trent Reznor’s Nothing label. His fashion work includes music for Alexander McQueen’s “Plato’s Atlantis” show and for the Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition “Punk: Chaos to Couture”. After “Pigmartyr” (2004) and a long pause, PIG returned on Metropolis Records with “The Gospel” in 2016 and has since released “Risen” (2018), the covers album “Candy” (2019), “Pain Is God” (2020), “The Merciless Light” (2022) and “Red Room” (2024), most of them paired with remix companions, the latest being “The Merciful Night” in 2025. The 2026 campaign began with the singles “Tosca’s Kiss” and “Sex & Suicide”, then the album “Hurt People Hurt” on 22 May, co-written with Davies and reviewed by Side-Line in July, followed by a Side-Line interview in August. Both new co-writers have PIG history: Watts and Heal released the “Compound Eye Sessions” EP together in 2015, and Schulz played on “Wrecked”. “Dirt Box” is the first PIG record to carry writing credits for both of them alongside Davies.

items.body: South London poet and DJ James Massiah supplies the voice on the new HAAi single. “I Wanna Feel Like Someone” is out today, 3 September 2026, on Mute, and it is the third track lifted from the album “DIGITiSE”, which the label releases on 9 October 2026 on vinyl, CD and digitally. The single arrives with an official visualiser and with a batch of new DJ dates, among them a 10-hour open-to-close set at Refuge in New York on 18 October and an all-night set at EartH in London on 31 October. DIGITiSE by HAAi HAAi, the London-based, Australian-born producer, songwriter and DJ Teneil Throssell, built the track out of her own time behind the decks. “‘I Wanna Feel Like Someone’ is a track that is purely made from memories of my sets over the years. It’s a nod to so much of the music I play and have played, and was a really fun track to make for the dance floor,” she said. She said the track “pushes the elements that I love most in dance music, bass and frequency, and ties it together with Motorik rhythms”, and described Massiah’s vocals as “an important anchor in the song” that gives it “a moment to breathe in amongst the textural heaviness.” Massiah, who already appeared on “All That Falls Apart” from her 2025 album “HUMANiSE”, commented: “Love working with HAAi, always grateful when an artist I respect finds a new way to present my voice.” The single follows the title track, shared in June alongside the album announcement, and “Ignition” featuring Echonomist, released in July. “DIGITiSE” runs to ten tracks: “RE-HUMANiSE” (feat. Kaiden Ford and ILA), “Printerlude”, “Ignition” (feat. Echonomist), “Depth Perception”, “DIGITiSE” (feat. Pat Alvarez), “Technology”, “HUMANiSE Radio”, “THANK U”, “I Wanna Feel Like Someone” (feat. James Massiah) and “Talking Walls” (feat. Skybreak and Cantoalegre, a children’s choir from Medellin, Colombia). HAAi calls the record the “bigger, ravey sibling” of “HUMANiSE” and ties it directly to her DJ sets: “DIGITiSE was created with intention: I wanted to make music I could play when I DJ. I wanted it to sonically spread across multiple lanes in the way I would play an all night long set.” Martin Falck, who has worked with Fever Ray and The Knife, leads the visuals. The album is available to pre-order on Bandcamp and through Mute. HAAi DJ dates 2026 The New York and London dates are the two longest sets on the list. The full run, including several back-to-back (b2b) bookings, is: 4 September – Sheffield (UK), b2b Sam Alfred, Electric Loves: Mall Grab at Electric Studios 19 September – Ibiza (ES), Bugged Out 26 September – Brussels (BE), b2b DJ Tennis, Place Simon Bolivar 30 September – Ibiza (ES), b2b Sally C, Mau P at Pacha 9 October – Geneva (CH), Electron Festival 10 October – Manchester (UK), IPC curates b2b with DJ Seinfeld, The Warehouse Project 17 October – Miami, Florida (US), iiiPoints Festival 18 October – New York (US), Open to Close, Refuge 22 October – Manchester (UK), 20 Years of the Warehouse Project 23 October – Amsterdam (NL), b2b Adiel, Audio Obscura x Raw Factory 25 October – Athens (GR), b2b Romy, Eden 31 October – London (UK), HAAi All Night at EartH 18 December – Bristol (UK), b2b Special Request, Mastery x Glade at Prospect About HAAi Teneil Throssell grew up in Karratha, Western Australia, and played in rock bands before moving to the UK as one half of the psychedelic duo Dark Bells. She started DJing after that band split and held a two-year residency at the London club Phonox from late 2016. The debut EP “Systems Up, Windows Down” came out on Mute on 14 November 2019, and the debut album “Baby, We’re Ascending” followed on the same label on 27 May 2022, with guests including Jon Hopkins. In 2023 she compiled an edition of the “DJ-Kicks” series for !K7 and released “Lights Out” with Fred again.. and Romy. The second album, “HUMANiSE”, was released on Mute on 10 October 2025, preceded by “Can’t Stand To Lose”, “Shapeshift” (with KAM-BU), “Satellite”, “Hey!” and “Stitches”. Massiah’s vocal on “All That Falls Apart” from that record is the link to the new single. “DIGITiSE”, announced in June 2026, picks up where “HUMANiSE” stops: the choir that closes the 2025 album returns on the opening track of the new one. “I Wanna Feel Like Someone” is the third single from the album, just over five weeks before the album arrives and eight weeks before HAAi’s all-night set at EartH.
