items.body: Six years after the first volume, the Austrian label TORM Ent. has announced Tormentum Volume II, a 2CD compilation of 26 tracks made with the German industrial and noise imprint L.White Records. The label describes it as “An uncompromising journey into the outer reaches of industrial, noise, power electronics, experimental sound and sonic extremity.” Pre-orders run by email to the label rather than through a shop or a Bandcamp page. The tracklist is exclusive or selected material from Black Leather Jesus, Sshe Retina Stimulants, Institution D.O.L., Sutcliffe No More, Adolphobitch, Code Neda, Edge Of Decay, Monocromática, Mezire, Kleistwahr, Hiroyuki Chiba, Dagda Mor, Rope Society, Torturing Nurse, Fire In The Head, Mademoiselle Bistouri, Stahlwerk 9, Wuornos Aileen, Manifesto, Pffft…!, coH, Sektion C, Morgue Ensemble, Höllenfürst, Augmented Atrocity and Jaw Surgery. Per-track titles have not been published. What is on ‘Tormentum Volume II’ The roster reads as a cross-section of four decades of extreme electronics. Black Leather Jesus is the harsh noise collective Richard Ramirez started in Texas in 1989. Sutcliffe No More is Kevin Tomkins and Paul Taylor, continuing under a new name since they ended Sutcliffe Jugend at the close of 2019. Kleistwahr is Gary Mundy of Ramleh and Broken Flag, a project he ran from 1982 to 1987 and revived in 2009. Torturing Nurse have worked out of Shanghai since April 2004 and run the Shasha Records label there. coH is Ivan Pavlov, Russian-born and resident in Sweden since 1995. Sshe Retina Stimulants is Paolo Bandera of Sigillum S, running since 1993. Fire In The Head is Michael Page’s solo project, going since early 2004. Monocromática is Valentina Artaud, working from Montevideo. Institution D.O.L., Adolphobitch and Höllenfürst all have records on TORM Ent. itself. Institution D.O.L.’s LP “Agape :93:” came out on the Norwegian label Edged Circle Productions on 23 January 2026 in a scarlet-vinyl edition of 300, and Adolphobitch’s CD “Eros Erotique Ephemere” followed on the same label on 2 March 2026, also limited to 300. Volume I set the pattern. TORM Ent. issued it on 1 November 2020 as a 2CD limited to 300 copies in a six-panel digipak, also 26 tracks, with Bastard Noise, The Rita, Schloss Tegal, ANTIchildLEAGUE, Uncodified, Hiroshi Hasegawa, Control, Caligula031, Fuckhead and Opening Performance Orchestra among the contributors. Institution D.O.L., Adolphobitch, Höllenfürst and Fall Into Dry Lungs appear on both volumes. About TORM Ent. TORM Ent. runs from Austria under the line “Austrian Industrial Culture since 1997”. Its own account of the start is direct: “Established in 1997 TORM Ent. started as small, independent concert and event label. In the beginning the focus was on extreme metal music stuff, hand in hand with Industrial/EBM/Electro styles.” It has worked as a promoter as much as a label, staging shows at STWST and Kapu in Linz and running the Tormentum Festival there in 2022, 2023 and 2024. The record catalogue is short and deliberate. It opened in 2000 with Institution D.O.L.’s “(Cultural) Death By Consumism / Die Macht”, the solo power electronics project Barbie B. founded in 1998 and has fronted since, latterly with Meta Dolor. TORM Ent. then issued Institution D.O.L.’s “Our Love Can Destroy This Whole Fucking World” on LP and CD in 2019 and “The Thelema Tales” on CD in 2020, Höllenfürst’s numbered gatefold 2LP “7” in November 2019 in an edition of 300, Adolphobitch’s “Broken Wings” CD in 2020, the first “Tormentum” compilation later that year, and a 2025 double cassette split live recording by The Rita, Black Leather Jesus, JSH, Vomir and Fall Into Dry Lungs. L.White Records is a German label with more than 160 releases, several of them by artists on the new compilation, including Torturing Nurse, Mezire, Sektion C and Black Leather Jesus. Side-Line last covered the label in March 2025, when it reissued a 2023 Chinese noise and industrial compilation. Institution D.O.L. and Adolphobitch live dates TORM Ent. has confirmed five shows for its two main acts: 2 October 2026 – Linz, Austria – Cinematograph – Institution D.O.L. 31 October 2026 – Linz, Austria – Alte Welt – Adolphobitch 28 November 2026 – Prague, Czech Republic – Mythology – Adolphobitch 16 April 2027 – Budapest, Hungary – venue to be announced – Institution D.O.L. 29 May 2027 – Antonin, Poland – Klub Szperek, Defibrylator Fest 12 – Institution D.O.L. The label is also taking pre-orders in person at Tower Transmissions XII in Dresden, the two-day experimental music event running 25 and 26 September 2026 at Reithalle Strasse E with Prurient, Dernière Volonté, Linekraft and Ke/Hil on the bill.

items.body: Carlos Vergara, singer and bassist of Barcelona post-punk trio Low Blows, made the video himself this time. “SOS” comes out as a single with that video on 15 September 2026. The song is not new to the band’s catalogue: it is the second track of the self-titled album “Low Blows”, released on 9 January 2026, and now gets its own single release. The band describe the video as “a dreamlike and hypnotic piece reflecting the feelings of life, loss and companionship that run through the song.” Low Blows by Low Blows “SOS” sits between the opener “Vacío” and “Fix Me” on the ten-track album, which runs on to “Misleading Blind (Album Mix)”, “Cracks”, “Intermezzo”, “I Hate (Album Mix)”, “Overrated”, “Go! (Album Mix)” and “Fin”. Low Blows recorded the album throughout 2024 and 2025 in their homes, their practice room and at Estudi Nautilus, where Jordi Solans handled the recording. Matteo Vallicelli, drummer of The Soft Moon, produced it, Lluis Cots mixed it at Estudi Nautilus and Maurizio Baggio mastered it at La Distilleria. Irina Stanciulescu did the artwork and design and Eduardo Cañas took the band photographs. ‘SOS’ follows ‘Vacío’ and a remix release The single is the second the band pull from the album. Side-Line covered the first in January: Low Blows release ‘Vacío’, first single and video from self-titled 2026 album, with a video directed by Marta Szewczyk. Between the two singles, on 29 May 2026, Low Blows put out “Remixes”, a four-track set with “SOS – doomzdei Remix”, “Misleading Blind – Matteo Vallicelli Remix”, “Vacío – SARCOMA Remix” and “Go! – LADIVINA Remix”. The new video for “SOS” is in-house work: Vergara made it himself, and the band signed the announcement as “Carlos & Low Blows”. About Low Blows Low Blows began in the mid-2010s as the solo project of Chilean musician Carlos Vergara, then living in Ibiza after his earlier bands Federación de Boxeo and This Co. The first two EPs, “Holes To Fill” (2016) and “Flesh” (2017), came out on the Manchester label Sister 9 Recordings and built on programmed electronics and guitars; a self-released digital EP, “Beyond The Flesh”, followed in 2018. The move to Barcelona turned the project into a band, with Rubén Carballo on drums, Andrés Silgado of Venus Fly Trap on guitar and, for a time, Marcel Molina on keyboards, alongside Vergara on bass and vocals. A run of singles from 2019 onwards, among them “Stranger”, “Low Blows” and “Skin”, led to the debut album “Cruel”, released in April 2020 on the Barcelona label Siete Señoritas Gritando. The standalone track “Ficción” appeared in 2021, followed by “Hate”, “Misleading Blind” and “I Hate” in 2023, and the singles “Normal” and “Go!” in 2024. The band’s own line for the sound is “post-punk for a hype, hyper, post and lost era”, and the songs mix post-punk, darkwave, industrial and new wave elements with lyrics in both Spanish and English. The self-titled second album, released on 9 January 2026 and produced by Matteo Vallicelli, gathered album mixes of “I Hate”, “Misleading Blind” and “Go!” with new material such as “Vacío”, “SOS” and “Cracks”. Low Blows now work as a trio of Vergara, Carballo and Silgado, and “SOS”, out as a single with its video on 15 September 2026, is the second track they lift from that record.

items.body: Luigi Pirandello’s idea that a person is a set of masks rather than a single self supplies the theme of the first single by Giuliana May. The Italian singer released “Who am I?” on 6 March 2026 through Saturno Dischi, as a one-track digital single of two minutes and 46 seconds, and followed it on 13 March with an official video. The song is out on Spotify, Deezer and the other main streaming platforms. Her press office describes the record as “dark-ethereal / cinematic pop”, and the track sets close-miked vocals against a string-led orchestral arrangement. Alongside Pirandello, the lyrics reference Modernist literature; T.S. Eliot and Samuel Beckett are the other names the artist cites. Giuliana May wrote the song with Marco Poletto, the Florence-based songwriter and producer who records as nonpiangere, and Poletto produced it. Ivan Mazzone wrote and directed the video, with Diego Vitale as director of photography, editor and colourist and Raffaele Chiantese on 2D animation and compositing. The team shot it in the woods of Piana del Dragone at Volturara Irpina, in the Irpinia hills east of Naples, with the support of the local municipality and Pro Loco. The cover image comes from the visual artist Xander Cicalese, known as icarvsfilm, who has also built a series of analogue collages around the song: handwritten verses, paper cut-outs and portrait fragments sewn together with needle and red cotton thread. The Italian art magazine Exibart covered those collages in a feature in August. ‘Who am I?’ as a teaching resource The single comes with a “Who am I?” Multidisciplinary Educational Suite that uses the song to teach art, literature and philosophy. Tune into English, a platform that teaches English through pop songs, has published a worksheet built on the track, and the teacher network Freeed has run an article on the suite. Coverage of the single so far has also come from The LA Note Magazine in the United States, from Il Corriere del Mezzogiorno, which profiled the artist in its print edition of 22 March 2026, and from the business daily Il Denaro. About Giuliana May Giuliana May is a singer, songwriter and sound designer from the Naples area in southern Italy. She holds a master’s degree in Science of the Show Business and trained in music production and music branding at the SAE Institute, IED Milan and the Venice Biennale’s CIMM, and graduated from the BigRock/H-Farm programme. “Who am I?”, released on 6 March 2026 on Saturno Dischi and written with its producer Marco Poletto, is her first release under her own name; the official video, directed by Ivan Mazzone, followed on 13 March. No Discogs or Wikipedia entry exists for the artist at the time of writing, and the single is her only title on the streaming platforms. Links to her channels are collected at linktr.ee/giulianamay.

items.body: After two self-released albums, Bagger 258 have a label. “Der Technokrat”, a two-track digital single, came out on August 28, 2026 through Scanner, the Dark Dimensions imprint that also handles The Saint Paul, Resistor and Akalotz. The Augsburg EBM duo of Nico von der Eisenmühle and Tim Schmelzer pair the original (3:31) with “Der Technokrat (The Saint Paul Edit)” (3:45), reworked by label-mate The Saint Paul. The single is available to stream and download on Bandcamp, where it sits in the Scanner catalogue alongside the label’s other 2026 releases, and on the usual streaming services. There is no physical edition. Der Technokrat by Bagger 258 What ‘Der Technokrat’ is about The band describe the song as a story in two halves: an authority that demands obedience, then a workforce that stops obeying. In the label notes they write that the track “explores the conflict between totalitarian control and individual resistance within an industrialized system” and that “the initial oppression gives way to open revolt: the working class refuses to comply, dismantles the existing power structures, and confronts the corrupt leadership with a collective claim to self-determination.” The theme continues the factory-floor vocabulary that runs through the Bagger 258 catalogue, from the albums “Ode an die Arbeit” and “Aufwärts gehts bergab”, where track titles include “Arbeiterwut”, “Werkshalle 4” and “Schicht im Schacht”. Musically the duo stay with the stripped-down, bassline-led EBM they have used since their debut. The label notes describe the track as built on “a relentless, machine-driven foundation of pounding beats, forceful basslines, and a dark, high-energy atmosphere”. “Der Technokrat” is the first new Bagger 258 material since the second album “Aufwärts gehts bergab”, released on February 20, 2026, and the first Bagger 258 release to appear on Scanner. The duo had already remixed for the label: their version of “The Undertaker” by Gamma Vortex came out through Scanner in September 2025. About Bagger 258 Bagger 258 formed in Augsburg, Germany as the EBM duo of Nico von der Eisenmühle and Tim Schmelzer, both also members of Projekt 26. They set out to revive the direct, bass-driven style associated with Anhalt EBM. In a Side-Line interview Schmelzer said they “were on a mission to resurrect something no one seemed to be messing with anymore – that punchy, in-your-face Anhalt EBM”. Von der Eisenmühle summed up the Bagger 258 method in the same conversation: “we’re after basslines that make you stomp, a brutal vibe, and tunes that stick with you.” The self-released debut album “Ode an die Arbeit” came out on November 24, 2023, mixed by Daniel Hallhuber of Young & Cold Records in Augsburg and mastered by Stefan Poiss of Mind.In.A.Box, and reached first place in the Deutsche Alternative Charts. Side-Line reviewed it in February 2024 and interviewed the duo the following month. Two digital singles followed in 2024: “Körperkommando” on June 21, with remixes by Kreign, Tension Control and Gamma Vortex, and “Alter Mann” on November 19. Both title tracks were carried over to the second album. “Aufwärts gehts bergab” arrived on February 20, 2026 as a digital release and a CD digipak limited to 258 copies, mixed and mastered by Krischan Jan-Eric Wesenberg at Studio 600 in Gelsenkirchen, Its thirteen tracks run “Arbeiterwut”, “Alter Mann”, “Funktion, Kontrolle!”, “Werkshalle 4”, “Erzengel”, “Körperkommando”, “Exakt!”, “Body 258”, “…und der Rest ist Geschichte” and “Schicht im Schacht”, closed by remixes of “Werkshalle 4” by Nachtmahr, of “…und der Rest ist Geschichte” by NordarR and of “Body 258” by Menticide. The duo play Nocturnal Culture Night 19 in Deutzen on the weekend of September 4-6, 2026. Both albums and the 2024 singles remain available through the band’s own Bandcamp page, separate from the Scanner catalogue that hosts the new single. “Der Technokrat” moves the project from self-release to the Scanner / Dark Dimensions roster.

items.body: Cicero, the Scottish synthpop artist whom Pet Shop Boys signed to their Spaghetti Recordings label in the early 1990s, has remixed Danish synthpop duo SoftWave. “Wake Up (Cicero Remix)” comes out on 18 September 2026 as a self-released digital single, mastered by Nordic Music Group, with cover artwork by Jason Stetson. A pre-save link is live. The remix returns a favour. SoftWave’s friend and collaborator Barney Ashton-Bullock, working for Cherry Red, introduced the duo to Cicero, and SoftWave went on to remix his 1992 single “Love Is Everywhere”, a track produced by Pet Shop Boys with Neil Tennant on backing vocals. Their version appeared on 29 September 2023 on the 3CD 30th anniversary expanded edition of Cicero’s album “Future Boy”, where it sits on the “Ciceroddities!” disc next to four other new remixes of the song and live recordings from Heaven in 1991. Three years later Cicero takes the controls for SoftWave. The duo describe his version as one that “brings a distinctive retro synthpop and Italo-disco flavour to the track, while preserving the melody and emotional core of the original.” “Wake Up (Cicero Remix)” is the second of three singles leading up to “things we’ve remixed”, SoftWave’s remix album due on 23 October 2026. The first was “Supernova (Aspra Remix)”, released on 21 August 2026 and made by Aspra, the solo project of Marsheaux’s Sophia Sarigiannidou. The album collects nine remixes by producers from six countries and marks more than a decade of the duo’s collaborations. From ‘Aspire’ to ‘things we’ve remixed’: the history of ‘Wake Up’ The original “Wake Up” first appeared on the five-track EP “Aspire”, released digitally on 14 October 2022 and reviewed on Side-Line as “Aspire”. SoftWave described it at the time as the song for people who cannot get out of bed early. A year later the track was carried over to the album “things we’ve done”, out digitally on 13 October 2023, on CD through Electro-Shock Records on 20 October 2023 and on vinyl on 21 June 2024. Jerry Olsen wrote the music and played the synthesizers, Catrine Christensen sang and wrote the lyrics, and Nordic Music Group’s Jacob Cederberg mixed and mastered the album. A remix compilation after every release has become a habit for the duo. “Together Alone The Remixes” (2017) followed the debut EP with nine remixes from six countries, and “Game On 1Up” (2019) reworked the debut album with twelve remixers, among them former Human League member Ian Burden. “things we’ve remixed” is the third such collection. About SoftWave SoftWave formed in Denmark in 2014 as the duo of Catrine Christensen (vocals, lyrics) and Jerry Olsen (synthesizers, production), working out of their own Blue Orange Studio. They mix classic British-styled synthpop with dance-pop and name Erasure as an inspiration. The debut EP “Together Alone” came out on 27 May 2016, followed by “Together Alone The Remixes” on 15 February 2017 and a remake of “Everything Change” for the Danish Electro Vol. 01 compilation in February 2018. The debut album “Game On” arrived in April 2019 on digital, LP and CD, preceded by the singles “Something Is Missing”, “No Need To Hide” and “Galaxy Of Stars”; Side-Line reviewed the vinyl edition of “Game On”. The remix album “Game On 1Up” followed on 19 November 2019 and was reissued on CD by Electro-Shock Records on 1 October 2020 with a live bonus track recorded at Rockefeller in Oslo, where SoftWave supported OMD on the Scandinavian leg of the “Souvenir” tour in February 2020 (Side-Line review: “Game On 1Up”). In 2021 the duo produced two remixes for Andy Bell‘s “Club Torsten!” LP on Cherry Red, and on 11 June 2021 they released the single “System Failure”. The EP “Aspire” (14 October 2022) was followed by the Christmas single “Will It Ever Be Christmas Again” on 1 December 2022, co-written with Barney Ashton-Bullock, and by the second album “things we’ve done” in October 2023. That same autumn SoftWave’s remix of “Love Is Everywhere” appeared on Cicero’s “Future Boy” expanded edition. A 12″ vinyl EP of the Christmas single, with a radio edit, an interview and a new remix, came out on 24 November 2025. The remix album “things we’ve remixed”, opened by “Supernova (Aspra Remix)” in August 2026 and continued by “Wake Up (Cicero Remix)” on 18 September, is due on 23 October 2026.

items.body: Sardinian dark disco and coldwave producer Matrukk released “Diavoleide” on Cat Cave Records on 28 August 2026. The digital single carries two takes on the same track, a long version and a short version, and is out on Bandcamp. Matteo Girometti, who records as Matrukk, produced the release and handled the additional mix, and is credited as executive producer. Valeria Black Val took the cover photograph, with Michele Manca as model and the shoot located at the Follesa house in Donori, Sardinia. Girometti did the cover graphics and post-production himself. Diavoleide by Matrukk What ‘Diavoleide’ follows in the Matrukk catalogue The single is the producer’s second Cat Cave Records release of 2026. It follows “In the Shadow of Neon Light”, issued on 22 May 2026, which Girometti composed and produced alone, with mastering by Matteo “Mr Bizz” Floris and cover photography again by Valeria Black Val. Before that came “Scary Female (Sbikka Dark Tech Groove Revibe)” on 10 April 2026, a rework of a track from his own catalogue. Both versions of “Diavoleide” run on the same material, with the long version giving the arrangement more room and the short version cut for shorter play. About Matrukk Matrukk is the recording name of Matteo Girometti, a producer and DJ born in Cagliari, Sardinia. He worked for the Rome record shop Goody Music before turning to production, and his releases mix dark disco, coldwave, darkwave and dark electronic material. His first release under the name, the two-track “Witches Screaming ep”, came out on 11 May 2025 and paired “Witches Screaming”, featuring Katarina Rose and f r a g i l e, with “Creepy Girl”, featuring Alesia Davina. Matteo “Mr Bizz” Floris mastered both tracks. The “Dark Night ep” followed on 5 October 2025 with “Dark Night”, featuring Katarina Rose, Sample_me and Dzerit, and a second version of “Scary Female” with Alesia Davina. Sbikka’s rework of “Scary Female” arrived in April 2026, and “In the Shadow of Neon Light” in May. “Diavoleide” is his fifth release in sixteen months and his second single of 2026. No album has been announced.

items.body: Three new tracks in thirteen minutes: that is the whole of “Melting Point X1”, the digital EP that Chainreactor released on August 28, 2026 through ProNoize, the Dark Dimensions imprint that has carried the project since 2009. The Düsseldorf industrial techno project of Jens Minor pairs the EP with an official video for the opening track, “Permagna”, which went up on the label’s YouTube channel the same day. The EP consists of “Permagna” (4:52), “Maybe, Maybe not” (4:30) and “S!ck Mode” (3:35). It is a digital-only release, available to stream and download on Bandcamp, where it is also part of the ProNoize label discography. Melting Point X1 by Chainreactor ‘Permagna’ and the sound of ‘Melting Point X1’ ProNoize presents the EP as a return to the project’s first records. The label text calls the three cuts “raw, hard-hitting, and unapologetically dirty” and says the EP “embraces the project’s original DNA: no gimmicks, no compromises”. Chainreactor has built its tracks on samples rather than sung vocals since “Interlinked” in 2020, after a period with Kay Schäfer as singer, and the label text places the new EP in that line. Side-Line has reviewed each of the last five Chainreactor albums and EPs, from “Interlinked” in 2020 to “War Machinery” in 2025. “Melting Point X1” is the second Chainreactor release of 2026 after the one-track digital single “Unintentional Presence – Part 2” on April 24, and the first EP since “The Essence” in 2021. It also continues a direction Side-Line noted on the last album: the “War Machinery” review described Minor as circling “back to his roots – delivering raw power through a perfect fusion of Dark-Electro, Industrial, and Rave”, with spoken-word samples in place of vocals. That twelve-track album, which includes “No Apologies”, “Roar”, “Go”, “Kalt” and “Unendlichkeit”, was the tenth in the Chainreactor catalogue. ProNoize is the harder electronic arm of Dark Dimensions, the German label group that also runs Scanner, and it has released every Chainreactor album since the 2009 debut. Its Bandcamp catalogue now lists 86 releases, and the new EP is sold there as a single digital download rather than as part of a physical edition. About Chainreactor Chainreactor started in 2009 as the solo project of German producer Jens Minor. The debut album “X-Tinction” came out on ProNoize the same year, followed by “Insomniac” (2011), “The Silence & The Noise” (2013), “Mass Driver” (2014), “Dirt” (2015) and “Decayed Values” (2017), all on the same label. Kay Schäfer joined as a second member and singer during that stretch, and a “Rare Stuff & Remixes” compilation collected loose tracks in 2017. Minor mixes hard techno, power noise, EBM and trance elements into a club-oriented industrial sound that he has called “a testing range where I can put all the influences of music that I like to something new” in a Side-Line interview. The seventh album, “Interlinked” (2020), dropped vocals again in favour of samples, a decision Schäfer, who had become a full member and the singer on the preceding albums, explained in that interview: “Chainreactor is about creating a certain atmosphere and feeling and this is done through the music itself and not through lyrics.” Videos for “Interlinked”, “Grey” and “The Wicked” accompanied that twelve-track album. The EP “The Essence” followed in 2021, then the albums “Techno Body Device” (2022), “Venom” (2023) and, as a solo project once more, “War Machinery” (2025), the tenth Chainreactor album. The digital singles “Welcome To The Deep” (four tracks) and “Destroyer Of Worlds” (two tracks) followed in 2024, then “Roar” and “30 Ghosts 2K25” in 2025, all of them on ProNoize. “Melting Point X1” follows “War Machinery” by a year and returns to the format of the project’s early, sample-driven records.

items.body: !K7 Records has handed its next DJ-Kicks mix to djrum. “DJ-Kicks: djrum” arrives on 16 October 2026 as a signed 2LP EcoRecord, a standard 2LP EcoRecord, a digipak CD and a digital album, and is available to pre-order. The London DJ and producer Felix Manuel mixed it live from vinyl on three turntables, then chopped, collaged and overdubbed the result in the studio. The mix carries four new djrum productions – “Turning”, “Psychic Video”, “Leave Me Alone” and “To Do What To Do” – alongside exclusive tracks by Skee Mask and Clark. “Psychic Video” is the lead single and is out now. DJ-Kicks: djrum by djrum The mix moves through ambient, classical, post-punk, acid, breakcore and percussive minimalism, and it runs on a thread of field recordings by Chris Watson, the sound recordist who co-founded Cabaret Voltaire in Sheffield in 1973 and left the group in 1981 to record for television. Three Watson pieces sit in the mix: “Glastonbury Ocean Soundscape” opens it, “El Divisadero” runs past the halfway mark and “Waiting (aka Adult Cheetah)” closes side D on vinyl. Between them djrum places Venetian Snares, The Raincoats, emptyset, upsammy, Bugge Wesseltoft and E Wata. “I like things to be a bit bumpy,” djrum said of the sequencing, “to have ups and downs and fck with expectations!”* Manuel described his studio process as “meditational”, and he named DJ Food, “who, I think, is my most revered DJ of all time”, as an influence on the record. The press release describes the single “Psychic Video” as “a convulsive, percussive-heavy roller of mind-bending electronics with chopped spoken word samples”. djrum’s ‘DJ-Kicks’ tracklist The vinyl edition runs 14 tracks across four sides: A1. djrum – “Turning” A2. Skee Mask – “Flip” A3. |||||||||||||||||||| – “Causalities” A4. djrum – “Psychic Video” B1. djrum – “Leave Me Alone” B2. E Wata – “U D S2S” B3. Chewlie – “Run” C1. Bugge Wesseltoft – “Flimmer” C2. The Raincoats – “Only Loved At Night” C3. Clark – “Clonk Dual” C4. djrum – “To Do What To Do” D1. Chris Watson – “Waiting (aka Adult Cheetah)” D2. Lino Capra Vaccina – “Antico Adagio” D3. Chris Watson – “El Divisadero” The CD, streaming and continuous-mix edition runs 33 tracks, adding a reprise of the opening Chris Watson piece and Susumu Yokota’s “Fearful Dream”: Chris Watson – “Glastonbury Ocean Soundscape” djrum – “Turning” Venetian Snares – “Miss Balaton” Uwalmassa – “Untitled 12” Clark – “Clonk Dual” Human Resources – “New T” djrum – “Psychic Video” Idris Ackamoor & The Pyramids – “Traponga” Atrice – “Hatara” Lino Capra Vaccina – “Antico Adagio” Susumu Yokota – “Fearful Dream” Lo.Sai – “Voi Siete Qui” Kimyan Law – “Chungwa” Core Self – “Suspiria” The Raincoats – “Only Loved At Night” Chris Watson – “Glastonbury Ocean Soundscape (Reprise)” djrum – “Leave Me Alone” Chewlie – “Run” Bugge Wesseltoft – “Flimmer” Chris Watson – “El Divisadero” emptyset – “Point” Planet Battagon – “Salacians Of Trans-Neptunia” Skee Mask – “Flip” Eli Keszler – “Sun” E Wata – “U D S2S” Chris Watson – “Waiting (aka Adult Cheetah)” |||||||||||||||||||| – “Causalities” Mark – “Incantation For The Protection Of JC” upsammy – “Relict” A.Fruit – “Measures of Dispersion” Sandro Mussida – “EEE” djrum – “To Do What To Do” Actual Proof – “Maybe We’ll Stay (Sileni Remix)” The unmixed download edition holds 31 tracks, the same running order minus the Chris Watson reprise and the Susumu Yokota track. The DJ-Kicks series began in 1995 with C.J. Bolland’s volume and has run on !K7 since, with Modeselektor and Eris Drew delivering the last two entries of 2025. djrum’s edition is the third of 2026, after those by Sofia Kourtesis and TEED. djrum live dates 2026 djrum has played Lowlands, Gare in Porto and Gravitate Festival over the past two weeks. The remaining dates run into the new year: 22 August – Lowlands Festival, Biddinghuizen, NL (played) 29 August – Gare, Porto, PT (played) 30 August – Gravitate Festival, Alandroal, PT (played) 4 September – Draaimolen Festival, Tilburg, NL 11 September – Tresor / Globus, Berlin, DE 13 September – Waterworks Festival, London, UK 23 October – Zeezout, Amsterdam, NL 23 October – Club Raum ADE, Amsterdam, NL 24 October – Open Ground, Wuppertal, DE 28 November – KANAL, Brussels, BE 4 December – Cialo, Wrocław, PL 1 January 2027 – RADION, Amsterdam, NL About djrum djrum is the project of Felix Manuel, a London DJ and producer who learned piano at seven, trained as a jazz pianist and started DJing after inheriting his mother’s jazz record collection. He began by playing bass music, ragga and jungle at London squat parties and hosted a monthly show on Sub.FM. His first records, the “Mountains” EP (2011) and a second EP, came out on 2nd Drop, the label that released his debut album “Seven Lies” in 2013. A trilogy of EPs and the singles “LA” and “Space Race” followed in 2015 and 2016, before he signed to R&S Records for the “Broken Glass Arch” EP in November 2017 and the second album “Portrait With Firewood” in 2018, on which cellist Zosia Jagodzinska joined his own piano improvisations. The 2019 double A-side “Hard To Say” / “Tournesol” on R&S carried his own term for the material, “ambient-gabber”. After a five-year gap he moved to Houndstooth, the Fabric-affiliated label, for the “Meaning’s Edge” EP in late 2024, which reached number 15 on the UK albums chart, and the third album “Under Tangled Silence” on 25 April 2025, which peaked at number 9 on the UK albums chart and topped the dance albums chart. He supported it with a 32-date tour including Fabric in London and Primavera Sound. The “I Wander” EP, a 16-minute composition presented as one continuous track on vinyl and as seven edits digitally, followed on Houndstooth on 14 August 2026. As a DJ he mixes from vinyl on three turntables, moving between dubstep, drum and bass, breakcore, techno, trip-hop, jazz and ambient within one set, and it is that set-building method that “DJ-Kicks: djrum” documents on record for !K7.

items.body: Twelve days after the first live single, Till Lindemann has put out a second. “Du hast kein Herz (Live In Kraków)” appeared on streaming platforms on September 2, 2026, together with a live video cut from the concert footage. It follows “Übers Meer (Live In Kraków)”, which arrived on August 21, and both tracks preview “Live In Kraków”, the concert album and film that Out Of Line releases on September 25, 2026. The recording comes from the TAURON Arena in Kraków on December 1, 2025, one of the closing arena dates of the “Meine Welt” tour, and the video was published on the Till Lindemann YouTube channel. “Du hast kein Herz” sits fourteenth in the nineteen-track running order of the audio editions, three positions before “Übers Meer”. The show was filmed with twenty 4K cameras, six GoPros, two 360-degree rigs and a drone, and the live album is available in DTS-HD Master Audio 5.1 and 7.1 and Dolby Atmos alongside the stereo mix. Where ‘Du hast kein Herz’ comes from The studio version of “Du hast kein Herz” is the fifth track on “Zunge”, the album Lindemann released himself on November 3, 2023 after suspending a planned Universal Music release. Lindemann wrote the lyrics and Sky van Hoff wrote and produced the music. “Übers Meer”, the first live single, comes from the same album, where it sits one track earlier. Till Lindemann reissued that album in 2025 as “Zunge 2025”, adding nine tracks, three of them previously unreleased, plus remixes. The two Till Lindemann live singles so far draw only on “Zunge” material; the Kraków set also includes songs from the Lindemann duo albums (“Skills in Pills”, “Fat”, “Praise Abort”, “Fish On”, “Golden Shower”, “Knebel”, “Allesfresser”, “Blut”, “Platz 1”), the 2021 single “Ich hasse Kinder” and “Und die Engel singen” from the “Meine Welt” EP. The “Meine Welt” tour ran through arenas in seventeen countries from late October 2025, with the Kraków date sitting between Vienna on November 29 and Budapest on December 2, and Aesthetic Perfection opening. The concert recording that came out of it, “Live In Kraków”, arrives as a DVD, a Blu-ray, a CD and Blu-ray digipak, a limited KiT, a black double LP, a gold double cassette and a set of collector editions, including a 4,000-copy fan box. The full format rundown and setlist are in the Side-Line announcement linked above; the Blu-ray is region-free and carries a 16 age rating. Pre-orders run through the Out Of Line shop, and the two live singles are on the usual streaming services. About Till Lindemann Till Lindemann, born in Leipzig on January 4, 1963, has been the vocalist and lyricist of Rammstein since the band formed in Berlin in 1994. His work outside the group started with Lindemann, the duo with Swedish producer Peter Tägtgren that released “Skills in Pills” on Warner in 2015 and “F & M” on Universal on November 22, 2019. Tägtgren left in November 2020. Lindemann continued under his own name with the single “Ich hasse Kinder” on May 31, 2021 and the self-released album “Zunge” on November 3, 2023, which he toured across Europe that November and December. Till Lindemann signed to Out Of Line in early 2025. The “Meine Welt” EP came out digitally on December 20, 2024 and physically on March 28, 2025, with CD remixes by Aesthetic Perfection and by Megabot featuring Zacky Vengeance of Avenged Sevenfold. A Hocico remix of “Und die Engel singen” followed in July 2025, and “Es brennt…” in March 2026, with alternate versions by Alex Terrible of Slaughter To Prevail and Greg Mackintosh of Paradise Lost. The “Meine Welt” tour took that material into arenas across 2025 and 2026, and the first edition of TILL FEST took place in Leipzig in 2025. “Du hast kein Herz (Live In Kraków)” is the second extract from the concert recording that closes that tour cycle on record, and the first Till Lindemann live album under his own name.

items.body: For this new EP, Serbian producer Goran Alavux has teamed up with the Dutch label New York Haunted. It features four tracks that quickly immerse the listener in Alavux’s brand of Dark-Techno. Two of the tracks are hard and dark, at times interwoven with Industrial sounds and occasionally infused with a touch of EBM. In my opinion, these are the stronger tracks. The other two tracks don’t sound bad, but they are a bit too repetitive for my taste and lack the same menacing quality. Alavux always has something to offer, consistently combining high productivity with quality. (Rating:7). Listen to “M 5.3”: NYH404 03 Alavux – M 5.3. by New York Haunted About Alavux Alavux is the main recording alias of Serbian producer Goran Alavuk, who also records as Solaris Path. Discogs lists his releases from 2008 onwards on labels including Twilight 76 Records, Vocode Records, Bass Agenda Recordings, Diffuse Reality, Bunker Records and his own 0ktag0n Records, where the “Underground Is Resistance” series appears. Side-Line reviewed Polar Light on Adriatiko Recordings in January 2026 and Underground Is Resistance on 0ktag0n Records in February 2026. “Illusions” was released by New York Haunted on 28 May 2026 as a download. The four tracks are “Illusions”, “Aerial”, “M 5.3.” and “Mutatio”. No production credits are listed on the Bandcamp page and the EP has no Discogs entry at the time of writing. It is the third Alavux release reviewed on Side-Line in 2026.

items.body: There is a considerable buzz around Showing Teeth with the project already collecting nearly a quarter of a million followers on Instagram. Throw in a recent cover interview with Kerrang! plus a support slot for Bring Me The Horizon at their huge show in Manchester's BEC arena, and it's fair to say expectations are high. The band is essentially a solo project (there is a band for live shows), with versatile singer/songwriter Addison being the sole creative mind behind everything on debut EP, A Fate Worse Than Loneliness.This may be Showing Teeth's debut EP, but the quality of production would tell you otherwise. Everything feels polished, driven and agonised over. However, as is often the case on debut releases, it is difficult to pin down a definitive sound, mainly due to the songwriting dipping toes into so many genres throughout the seven tracks on offer. Initially you're lured into thinking this is going to be a blast of frenetic death/metalcore, with opener “Bad Exchanges” blowing the doors clean off with its bludgeoning intensity. Think along the lines of Knocked Loose teaming up with Employed To Serve at their heaviest and you’re getting close. But, by the time you get to the soaring Ariana Grande-esque pop choruses on finale “Paradigm”, you might be a tad confused with what direction this project wants to go in.  Addison's vocal range is absolutely incredible and clearly the star of the show. Even before we get to the clean vocals her palette of screams are simply stunning. Whether it be guttural growls or high pitched rasps it's all delivered with energy and venom. I’m pleased the clean vocals are not implemented lavishly on every track, especially as there is so much variation in the screams. For example, there's plenty of spiky texture on “Labyrinth” without the, admittedly catchy as hell, angelic chorus. Djent-laden “Rip” uses them in a different way, with a fleeting cameo at the one minute mark, before returning for a suitably flourishing finale. “Make It Out” and “Shallow Grave” do feel like slight mis-steps and go too far down a predictable nu-metal path, but I’m sure I will be in the minority on this point as the more accessible vocals are definitely a huge part of the bands appeal. In fact, I’m going to completely contradict myself now, but I would have preferred “Paradigm” to be brave, ditch the screams entirely, and just embrace its pop anthem glory. It will be interesting to see which direction they decide to go in for their inevitable full length release, and I hope they manage to laser focus their sound while still holding on to the ferocity present on "Bad Exchanges". I have no doubt that Showing Teeth are going to blow up insanely big over the next 12-18 months and this can only be a good thing for extreme metal, especially if they act as a new gateway for kids to discover other heavy bands. That being said, this is an incredibly promising debut release showcasing a serious vocal talent that will likely be filling arenas in years to come.

items.body: The age-old adage: what do you get when Genesis's Steve Hackett and Marillion's Steve Rothery cross proggy paths? Hopefully you haven't been asking that question too long, since The Roaring Waves is the first instance of the duo collaborating studio-wise. Yes, Rothery joined Hackett during the latter's 2013 concert at the Hammersmith Odeon, but this marks the premiere point of studio cooperation. It's quite surprising that these two musicians, each with decades upon decades of expertise in adjacent fields, only released a project last Friday. Hackett's been silent since 2023's The Circus and the Nightwhale, and Rothery's last release, The Ghosts of Pripyat, is nine years Nightwhale's elder. Eight years in the making led up to this (which explains the dip in activity from the respective players), so it's about time some classic, guitar-driven prog came my way, and I'd never ignore an artistic couplet such as Hackett & Rothery, so follow me as we dive straight into The Roaring Waves. It comes as no surprise, considering the kith and kin that are two progressive rock guitarists, that the record is purely instrumental. Think of it comfortably, rather than a full-throttle, blistering shredfest akin to some breakaway Dream Theater endeavor. The Steves rely on textural atmospherics instead of masturbatory showiness to craft the record's concept: the "profundity of the sea". Don't bend your legs and widen your feet just yet–the two artists bring the ocean to you. Whether they do so through a steady rocking pattern or electronic-laden passages is up to the natural course of Mother Nature's vast waterscapes. While the idea is intriguing, Hackett and Rothery only periodically conjure the nautical imagery exhibited on the album's cover. While the masterful duo trade winding, melancholic notes over shifting drum patterns (see "Sandsend," "The Black Sea") or simple ambience ("K-129"), there aren't enough sonic tinges to communicate such an expansive, oceanic environment. Little nods, like the natural sound effects in the opening track "The Storm," or the electronic pitter-patter sprinkled throughout The Roaring Waves' bulk of songs, rein me in from deeming the LP a standard instrumental release.This brings up a talking point heavily debated within the rock and metal community. Are instrumental records boring? Intrinsically, they are, when considering the heaviness of the genre. Of course, ambient albums surely mustn't include lyrics, but should progressive rock? Plenty of classics, like Camel's The Snow Goose or Mike Oldfield's myriad of sprawling epics, benefit from the instrumental's activity. There's nothing stagnant about these examples, hence their cult fame. The Roaring Waves waits until the final song, "Pacific Coast Highway," to supply any rocking action, and even that doesn't honestly fit in with the sea-ness. The twangy rip from Hackett's harmonica and symphonic feel aren't choices I would've made to muster oceanic vibes, and for this excitement, I had to tread thirty-eight-or-so minutes of consoling yet unwavering waters. I didn't plunge to the depths of The Roaring Waves expecting a tsunami; more of a point break. Instead, my bark swayed gently, rendering the gumption I gathered unnecessary.They can play their water pans and layer keyboard upon synth, but I want more from these illustrious talents. Granted, I wasn't a huge fan of Marillion (or neo-prog, actually), and Genesis fell off for me, along with everyone else, when the 80s pop wave decimated prog. Hackett helped the band navigate some of the finest recordings of the 70s; however, he should've administered a larger dose of his vintage spirit with his guitarmate. Dexterously, this collaboration fell short, but if you need forty-five minutes of simple backing tunes, you'll find these waves better fit for your boat. The Roaring Waves (24-bit HD audio) by Steve Hackett, Steve Rothery

items.excerpt: The Internet is undefeated when it comes to complaining. Even more so when it comes to something super important like… a stoner doom band putting out a new record without a foundational member. I kid a little bit, but in gathering the pulse of the doom community over the last few weeks, it’s clear the announcement of Sleep’s new lineup and singles are going over like a fart in church for many fans. items.body: The Internet is undefeated when it comes to complaining. Even more so when it comes to something super important like… a stoner doom band putting out a new record without a foundational member. I kid a little bit, but in gathering the pulse of the doom community over the last few weeks, it’s clear the announcement of Sleep’s new lineup and singles are going over like a fart in church for many fans. I’m seeing everything from the silly and stubborn “No Pike, no Sleep” to extremely sophisticated barbs like “they should change the band name to Nap.” To be honest, I get why people are upset. Sleep has coughed up some of the very best the genre has to offer. I’ll argue that 2018’s The Sciences is the group’s crowning achievement, my default suggestion to anyone pursuing the genre, and an all-time personal favorite—all in no small part due to Matt Pike’s presence of magnificent riffitude and scuzzy guitar tone.No doubt shaking up the personnel in a three-piece is going to make a difference. Further souring the recent discourse is the “firing” of drummer Jason Roeder, now back in his rightful place with Neurosis. It’s apparent that Al Cisneros is calling the shots for Sleep, and while many have viewed this as some kind of power trip, I’d argue it would be far stranger to have an Al-less version of Sleep—or for him to start an entirely new band to play this style of music. The cynic in me says that if Hempispheres were released under a different name, the grumpiest of online grumps would dismiss it as “wannabe Sleep” or something. Whatever. Bands come and go, members change, and life goes on. There are multitudes of bands who’ve changed lineups and moved on from key members, and this is no different. Whatever idea one has about what this band is or should be isn’t tied to any single person, and I think that’s an important distinction to keep in mind when listening to this record.All that said, my outlook going into Hempispheres is probably sunnier than most. Enlisting former Shrinebuilder collaborator and Melvins sticksman legend Dale Crover is a wonderful, if not downright obvious choice. There’s history there, dude kicks like a mule, and he can groove with the best of ’em. On the other hand, filling Pike’s shoes with Bud Dupree (Void) is a surprising call. A speedy ’80s D.C. hardcore guitarist at the helm of the S.S. Slow & Low? Now this was certain to garner some attention, but I wasn’t clear on how this’d actually play out. Sure, Pike is no stranger to ferocity and speed, but this substitution on paper seemed like it could really shake things up. Does it?Well, the rollout for Hempispheres might have you thinking so. Lead single “Have Spacesuit Will Travel,” in particular the “(4:20 Flexi Edit),” is just about as boilerplate as Sleep can get. The production is more bass-forward, we get some sci-fi synths in the mix for a little character, but it’s a curious choice to introduce the new lineup—an (only) four-freakin-minute Sleep song? No substantial soloing? How can anyone couch-lock into something so brief? It all felt a little …off. Truth be told, this is corrected on the album cut—I knew there were some solos hiding from us—but I’m left wondering why the introduction to this new lineup was cut so short, literally. Oddly enough, the second single, “The Morrisist,” landed in the same fashion: another sub-five-minute, heavy-on-the-eerie-atmosphere diddy, replete with more cosmic synths and an Om-like meditative groove. Shortform Sleep, especially on the heels of the phenomenal and utterly indulgent forays of The Sciences, hinted at something else entirely: a dramatic change in direction. And yet, fortunately, that’s not the case.The title-track centerpiece wastes no time getting cooking with that crooked, lurching Sleep groove we all know and love. The creepy spacey synths return, just enough to lend some distinguishing presence (they pop up time and time again, and I kinda love it?), but more importantly, Dupree gets his chance to lend his own signature. I gotta say, I’m really feeling what this dude lays down, and I absolutely adore how you can hear his flavor come through in a format that actually gives him time to let loose. (Seriously, take 10 minutes and throw those Void EPs on to get a little micro-taste of what you’ll find here.) If he’s a chiller, more subdued player than Pike, he’s also a more patient and expressive one; there’s something weirdly dark and haunting about the tone he’s dialed in, and goddamn can he make that fucker scream when he climbs the fretboard. He meshes in nicely with the bass-forward production of Hempispheres. Where previous records had bass and guitar matching fire with fire, this record sounds more like IcyHot. Rest assured, the closing three minutes of those resin-coated leads in this title track are about as Sleep as it gets without being that Sleep: something to groove with, but more importantly, something worth getting lost in.This spirit continues throughout the remainder of the album. The groove again leads the way in the jammy “Arrival of the Industry Ships,” an eleven-minute whopper with this progressively deteriorating, blown-out bass that’s equal parts percussive and “holy shit” levels of fuckery at an appropriate high volume. Al and Bubba flex a bit on the jams here, something I hope is a peek at what to expect on the road (or maybe I’m just buzzin’ on the whole jam thing after seeing King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard cut loose at Field of Vision). Similarly, closer “Whole Wheat Mountain / Well Baked” instantly locks in on another ear-turning groove. Crover, like Roeder and others before him, balancing restraint and style, every fill matching pace and power. The riffing here is something old Sleep might’ve had a lil’ more oomph behind, and it’s one of the few times it feels like the production isn’t doing the song justice. And yet, when Dupree cuts in with a lead, it all seems to make more sense. The contrast in the guitars is super effective and, in a way, unlocks the angle they take on Hempispheres.This is a (more) groove-forward version of Sleep. I’ll admit, the riffs aren’t quite as delicious as they’ve been in the past, but these grooves fucking stick. Is it the best Sleep album, or, to ask another way, did you really think they’d ever top The Sciences? No. Is it still worth splurging on all the Indica you can get your mitts on for this record? Absofuckinglutely. So let’s hit the cliché buttons: first impressions aren’t everything, and expectation is the thief of joy. For real, give this one some time to sink in if your precious ears can handle the tonal shift. It’s apparent Bubba and Dale understand the assignment: this is unequivocally a Sleep record, but with a different atmosphere, a new planet to explore, if you will.. Ultimately, it’s the same Sleep, just a different strain. Hempispheres by Sleep Hemispheres is available digitally everywhere on September 3 via Third Man Records. (Strange there’s no vinyl, eh?) The comic book is also available for preorder via Third Man, due out September 22.

items.body: 会期：2026/06/12〜2026/06/17 アトリエ春風舎［東京都］ 作：山本正典 演出：山本正典＋原竹志 公式サイト：https://kotorikaigi.yangotonaki.com/2026/Gesuitou/ 『おかえりなさせませんなさい』が2025年の第69回岸田國士戯曲賞最終候補作にノミネートされ注目を集めたコトリ会議／山本正典。同作は第3回関西えんげき大賞で最優秀作品賞と観客投票ベストワン賞を受賞するなど高い評価を受け、劇団の代表作となった。そのコトリ会議の新作『この上のない下水筒』（作：山本正典、演出：山本正典＋原竹志）はしかし、これまでの作風の延長線上にありながら、劇団の新境地を示す作品となっている。 ある夜。東日出中ゴミ拾い部の元部員・朝倉くんの死を知った同じく元部員たちが彼の住んでいたアパートにやってくる。部員たちが顔を合わせるのは中学卒業以来28年ぶりのことだ。ゴミ拾い部の元部長で、ことあるごとに朝倉くんと対立していた木戸（阪本麻紀）、朝倉と親しくしながら、卒業後はゴミ拾い部のことを忘れたいと願い生きてきた磯部（のたにかな子）、いつも人の話を聞いていない朝倉派の尾田（原竹志）、そして朝倉派から部長派に寝返った小間井（花屋敷鴨）。ゴミ拾い部は何かしらの事件をきっかけに卒業を待たずして解散してしまったらしく、どうやら部員たちの間には、未だにそのことに起因するわだかまりがあるようだ。不在の朝倉を中心に久しぶりに再会した4人は思い出話を交わし互いの近況を尋ね合うが、ぎこちない会話はそこに強い不信が忍び込んでいるがゆえだろう。互いの不信が高まりゆくなか、やがて誰が置いたかわからない300万円が見つかって──。 ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ コトリ会議の作品はそのほぼすべての作品においてSF的な設定が導入されている。SFといってもその多くはハードなそれではなく、例えばほとんど脈絡なく思えるようなかたちで宇宙人や人間ではない登場人物が登場するような世界を舞台とする、SF風味とでも言うべきテイストのものだ。このSF的な設定はとぼけたセリフ回しと相まって、コトリ会議の「少し不思議」な唯一無二の世界観を作り上げている。『この上のない下水筒』も例外ではない。 実はこの作品にはもうひとりの登場人物がいる。不在の（遺体となって奥の部屋に安置されている）朝倉の部屋に置かれている仮の朝倉（山本正典）である。「安村先生が楽天で取り寄せ」て「いろいろあったから」と部員たちのために置いたのだというその仮の朝倉はしかし、本物とは「顔が全然違う」らしく、のっけから尾田に「もう少し本人に寄せようと思わなかったのかい」「顔だけでも似せないとただのおじさんじゃないか」と言われてしまう。セリフ回しともどもいかにもコトリ会議な展開である。 ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ さて、仮の朝倉は幽霊かクローンか、あるいはアンドロイドだろうかなどと思いながら観ていると、意外にも（？）仮の朝倉はこの作品の主題らしきものを体現する存在であることがわかってくる（いや結局のところアンドロイド（？）でもあるようなのだが……）。仮の朝倉が本物に似ていないという指摘はそのまま、28年ぶりに顔を見たのに棺の中にいるのが本物の朝倉だとどうして言えるのか、そもそも28年ぶりに会ったお互いが本人だとどうやってわかるのかという問いへと展開し、誰かの「本当の姿」を知ることなどできはしないのだという真理へと至るだろう。思いや思い出はすれ違い、それぞれが抱く人物像が「本人」と完全に一致することは決してない。たとえ朝倉が生きていたとして、周囲の人間が見ているのはどこまでいっても「仮の朝倉」でしかないのだ。 ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ ［撮影：河西沙織（壱劇屋）］ 少しずつ各自の事情や思いが明らかになっていくワンシチュエーションの一幕劇は、ホラーの雰囲気をまとったサスペンスとして展開し、そして現実へと着地する。くすりと笑ってしまうような「少し不思議」な設定をそのまま、私たちが対峙する現実、あるいは他者という「謎」を体現するものとして提示してみせた山本の筆は、これまでの作品で「少し不思議」な世界を立ち上げてきたそれともまた違った巧みさを見せていた。少し不思議な世界を立ち上げることに留まらないその筆の力を改めて示してみせたのだと言ってもいい。「現実」を描くには山本の筆のナイーブさは危うくもあるものの（例えば本作で木戸に対して尾田が放つ「きみが性転換手術を施した朝倉くんなんじゃないのか」というセリフはまったく許容できるものではない。現在は性転換手術という言葉ではなく性別移行手術という言葉が使われているし、そもそもトランスジェンダーを取り巻く現在の状況を考えれば面白おかしく使っていい言葉でないことは自明だろう）、コトリ会議／山本正典の描く物語のさらなる広がりに期待したい。 『この上のない下水筒』ではコトリ会議としては2022年の『全部あったかいものは』以来の東京公演が実現したが、次は早くも10月に吉祥寺シアターで行なわれるショーケース公演『ラブ・演劇博 ─こちらの演劇、とおくのまちから。─』への参加が決定している。「地方を拠点に活動する劇団を吉祥寺シアターに招き、ショーケース形式で上演を行う」この企画では兵庫拠点のコトリ会議に加えて宮城のMICHInoX、岩手の冷蔵庫ポルカの作品も上演される予定だ。 観賞日：2026/06/17（水） 関連記事 コトリ会議『おみかんの明かり』（芸劇eyes番外編vol.3.『もしもしこちら弱いい派 ─かそけき声を聴くために─』）｜山﨑健太：artscapeレビュー（2021年08月01日号） コトリ会議『しずかミラクル』｜山﨑健太：artscapeレビュー（2018年07月01日号）

items.album: foams & mesh

items.excerpt: Of the many things that make albums featuring John Butcher unique, I believe the most outstanding characteristic is not that he likes to play at unusual venues (caves, water reservoirs, oil tanks…), but rather the fact that every ensemble he plays with is so diverse and incomparable that it allows the listener to hear many different facets of his playing. items.body: Of the many things that make albums featuring John Butcher unique, I believe the most outstanding characteristic is not that he likes to play at unusual venues (caves, water reservoirs, oil tanks…), but rather the fact that every ensemble he plays with is so diverse and incomparable that it allows the listener to hear many different facets of his playing. In an interview with Brad Rose, Butcher said that when improvising, he likes to hear the musician behind the instrument, though it’s not important to him to hear the musicians putting themselves in the spotlight - on the contrary, he tends to seek subtlety. In general, he looks for musicians who have already developed a personal musical style and their own way of playing - something that truly feels like their own. It is therefore almost inevitable that the various ensembles he selects based on these criteria will possess a unique dynamic and sonic world. One of last year’s best albums was RARE , John Butcher’s duo with French pianist Sophie Agnel, with whom he had been playing quite frequently over the last few years. I especially liked their improvisational rigor and the relaxed, varied, and aleatoric moments. On RARE , I considered the pauses in the music to be the central element; on foams & mesh , it’s different, mainly due to Pascal Niggenkemper (bass) and Ståle Liavik Solberg (drums), because the two of them fill those gaps. Solberg, with whom Butcher has played since 2015 in many kinds of combinations, permeates the improvisation with his bone-dry and at times almost esoteric style, for example when he uses extended materials (especially in the quiet passages of the first track). This is complemented by Agnel’s trills, which she plays from inside the piano. Butcher contributes very delicate bird calls here, while Niggenkemper subtly saws at the very low strings of his bass. It feels as though one is listening to the goings-on in the courtyard of a Tibetan monastery. This can be heard around the 20-mark of the first, significantly longer improvisation on foam & mesh. Such passages contrast with highly expressive moments, in which the rhythm section performs in a demanding and driving manner, but Butcher remains unflappable and employs his entire repertoire - guttural sounds, chirps, tremolos, circular breathing, serial/repetitive patterns, etc. - with casual ease. Only at the end of the track Agnel’s clusters and crescendos, Niggenkemper’s alienated drones and Solberg’s accentuated interceptions tempt him into vibrato-heavy phrases. The album was recorded at the artacts festival in St. Johann/Austria in 2024 and in the first part of the encore the musicians showcase extended playing techniques, with Niggenkemper and Agnel holding the improvisation together by a somber drone. Then the bass and piano shift imperceptibly into their normal registers, and the piece grows denser, builds in intensity, becoming louder and more concentrated - like a tornado - before dissolving perfectly. foam & mesh is an extraordinary album, the band is a superb match. They have played only three concerts so far and I think I’m not the only one who hopes that there will be more to come. foam & mesh is available as a CD and as a download. You can buy and listen to the album on the label’s website: https://sluchaj.bandcamp.com/album/foam-mesh foam & mesh by B:A:N:S BAND: Sophie Agnel / John Butcher / Pascal Niggenkemper / Ståle Liavik Solberg Email This BlogThis! items.excerpt: 日本の前衛芸術の鬼才・水野修孝の電子音楽を集成したCDがリリースされた。中でも“怒りの日”と題されたコンクレート作品は〈この作品は大音量で再生しなければならない〉という作曲者自身の指示が残されていることで知られる。去る6月、私とスリーシェルズはこの作品を文字通り大音量で再生するリスニングイベントを開催。当日はタンノイで普段の約3倍、100dB近い爆音で再生した。それはまさに音の斬撃そのもの。音が波であることを改めて実感すると共に、この作品はイヤホン等で聴くものではなく、大きなスピーカーを通して全身で浴びるように体感してこそ真価を発揮するのだと確信した。

items.body: Label: Calligram Records, 2026 Personnel - Geof Bradfield: tenor and soprano saxophone, bass clarinet; Ben Goldberg: clarinet, contra alto clarinet; Myra Melford: piano; Dana Hall: drums. What a wonderful time I had listening to this fantastic bass-less quartet, whose powerful avant-garde jazz captivates from start to finish. Recorded live at Chicago’s legendary Green Mill, Open or Close gathers compositions from all four members—saxophonist Geof Bradfield, clarinetist Ben Goldberg, pianist Myra Melford, and drummer Dana Hall—who, having crossed musical paths before in several contexts, make a remarkable debut as a group here. Ornette Coleman’s “ Open or Close ” is the stunning opener, showcasing a memorable eight-note riff that gradually evolves into staccato activity resembling rhythmic shocks of vibrant color. Initially, Melford constructs melodies around that riff, with Hall’s percussive driving force as her sole support. Goldberg’s sinewy clarinet phrasing also prompts quick responses from the drummer and effective comping from Melford; then Bradfield offers an earthy, motivic solo packed with tension and release before the theme returns. Melford’s “ A Line With a Mind of Its Own ”, inspired by American painter and sculptor Cy Twombly, is built over an exquisite scale, patiently expressed as a chamber-jazz concerto with moderate snare-drum effervescence, accelerations, and mounting intensity. The pianist also contributes the adventurous “ The Kitchen ”. Goldberg also brings two contrasting yet extremely effective compositions: “ Study of the Blues ” is definitely not your standard model within the genre, but rather a slightly dissonant exploratory piece with a lot of interesting things going on; “ Three Ingredients ”, on the other hand, is a bop-inflected piece centered on an expeditious figure. Starting as a conversation between contra-alto and bass clarinets, the tune evolves into a sort of avant-garde ragtime. The groove-forward standouts are marvelous to witness, and they provide a setting in which each musician’s distinct personality emerges naturally. Bradfield’s “ No Brand ”, a dedication to South African pianist Abdullah Ibrahim, flows with a feel-good, six-beat contra-alto clarinet groove, hi-hat buoyancy, and melodic discernment fueled by the parallel motion created by soprano sax and piano. During Goldberg’s beautifully articulated statement, there is no disruption to the groove in the lower register as he and the pianist switch roles. By the end, Bradfield and Melford mirror each other in thrilling interplay. Another dedication to a South African musician, bassist Johnny Dyani, comes with “ Lonely Flowers ”, a piece Dyani wrote himself and first recorded in 1978. These African scents also bring a touch of Sun Ra’s exoticism into play, and I love Bradfield’s fierce improvisational spirit here on tenor. Brimming with creative ideas, Open or Close has no weak tracks, with each one evoking thoughtful moods and sonic stimulation. These four musicians reveal exceptional musical capabilities, and their collective effort comes highly recommended. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Open or Close ► 03 - No Brand ► 04 - Study of the Blues ► 06 - Lonely Flowers

Limp Bizkit, St. Vincent, Fontaines D.C. & More Announced For Lollapalooza India 2027

3 September 2026

Lollapalooza India has announced the line-up for its next edition, which takes place at Mumbai's Mahalaxmi Race Course on January 23-24, 2027.

The 2-day event will host British singer Olivia Dean, nu-metal band Limp Bizkit, pop group KATSEYE, Irish post-punk band Fontaines D.C., Australian pop-rock band 5 Seconds of Summer, art-rock icon St. Vincent, Swedish House Mafia's Steve Angello and ¥ØU$UK€ ¥UK1MAT$U as some of the top draws this year. They'll be joined by UK singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri, Australian rock artist Ecca Vandal, US band Pinkshift, guitarist-producer Alain Johannes, Indonesian singer Isyana Sarasvati and Belgian duo 2manydjs, along with a one-off collaborative set from The Police's Stewart Copeland and composer Ricky Kej.

Homegrown talent on the lineup includes Aditya Gadhvi, Anuv Jain, Rajasthani folk theatrical production The Manganiyar Seduction, Zulan, Indian Ocean, BlackStratBlues, Kayan, Rhea Raj, Scribe, Maneesh On The Beat, RANJ x CLIFR, Swadesi, Yashraj, Varijashree Venugopal, Donn Bhat, Shanka Tribe, Rafiki, Curtain Blue, Run It's The Kid, Janisht Joshi, The Lightyears Explode, Meewakching, Calcutta Cowboy, Anoushka Maskey, Dohnraj & The Peculiars, Rasa, Noni-Mouse, Karshni, Raj and Shriya Rao.

For more information, follow Lollapalooza India.

items.body:
DMC World DJ Championships Return To India After 12 Years This Weekend

3 September 2026

After a 12-year hiatus, the DMC World DJ Championships are returning to India, with the national finals taking place at antiSOCIAL Mumbai on September 6.

Founded in 1985 as the Disco Mix Club, DMC is the longest-running global DJ competition, built around turntablism and the technical craft of DJing. Its championships have become a defining platform for scratch, beat juggling, cutting and other forms of turntable performance, with past winners including A-Trak, DJ Craze, DJ Kentaro, Q-Bert and Mixmaster Mike.

The India finals will feature two categories: the original DMC Classic Battle, which tests technical skill, creativity and musicality across a six-minute routine, and the Scratch Battle, dedicated entirely to scratch technique. Winners will earn the opportunity to represent India at the World Finals in London later this year.

The return of the competition and its culture in India is being led by DJ Uri alongside The Spindoctor, DJ Mocity and DJ Kan-i, with international champions DJ Fummy, Prime Cuts and Lobito Brigante appearing as judges and performers at the event. The day will also include workshops, equipment showcases and an afterparty.

For more details, head here, and get your tickets here. Check out DJ Fummy's winning set from 2025's world championship below to get a sense of what to expect:

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”
